title: Batteries, electrolysis and rust: what happens when a metal gives away electrons

summary.text: Push a zinc-coated nail and a copper wire into a lemon. A pair of earphones joined to them will crackle. The lemon holds no electricity. The zinc gives away electrons, and they travel through the wire to the copper. Your child tests which pairs of metals work. Then they use four AA cells to rust a nail in ten minutes and to split water into two gases. They find that a battery, split water and rust are one kind of change. In each, electrons move from one substance to another.
summary.art: Half a lemon on a plate with a grey nail and a copper wire pushed into it, and a pair of white earphones whose plug touches the nail.

intro.hook: A lemon has no battery inside it. So how can a lemon make a pair of earphones crackle?
intro.text: A lemon alone does nothing to a pair of earphones. A lemon with two copper wires does nothing either. But a lemon with one copper wire and one zinc-coated nail makes the earphones crackle. In this unit you find out why the two metals must be different. You also make a steel nail rust in ten minutes, and split water with four AA cells. All three happen for the same reason. The cells you use are small ones, and you never use electricity from a wall socket.
intro.art: A child with earphones in her ears touching the earphone plug to a nail that sticks out of half a lemon, looking surprised.

outcomes: I can build a lemon cell and say what the two metals, the juice and the wire each do.
I can explain why the two metals must be different, using the metal ladder.
I can explain that the metal giving away electrons is used up, which is where a battery's energy comes from.
I can say what volts measure, and why cells joined in a row push harder.
I can explain how an electric current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen.
I can explain why iron rusts, and why salt water makes it rust faster.
I can explain three ways to stop rust, including a coat of zinc.
I can plan a fair test with two metals, and say what my results show.

terms.meaning: A very tiny particle with a minus charge. Every atom has electrons. An electric current in a wire is a flow of electrons.
terms.example: When earphones crackle on a lemon cell, electrons are passing through their wires.
terms.art: A copper wire drawn large, with small dots marked with minus signs moving along inside it in one direction.

terms.meaning: An atom that has lost or gained electrons, so it carries a charge. Ions can move about in water and in juice.
terms.example: A zinc atom that gives away two electrons becomes a zinc ion and floats off into the lemon juice.
terms.art: A grey nail in yellow juice, with small grey balls marked with plus signs drifting away from the nail.

terms.meaning: A cell is two different substances and a liquid or paste between them, which together push electrons round a wire. A battery is two or more cells joined together.
terms.example: One AA cell is a cell. Four lemon cells joined in a row make a battery.
terms.art: One AA cell on the left, and four lemon halves joined in a row by wires on the right.

terms.meaning: A piece of metal or carbon that carries electrons into or out of a liquid.
terms.example: In a lemon cell the zinc nail and the copper wire are the two electrodes.
terms.art: A glass of water with two pencil leads dipping into it, each one labelled with an arrow.

terms.meaning: A liquid or paste with ions in it. The ions carry charge through it.
terms.example: Lemon juice and salt water are electrolytes. Cooking oil is not.
terms.art: Three small bowls labelled lemon juice, salt water and oil, with a tick on the first two and a cross on the third.

terms.meaning: The unit that tells how hard a cell pushes electrons.
terms.example: A lemon cell pushes with about 0.9 volts. An AA cell pushes with 1.5 volts.
terms.art: An AA cell with 1.5 V printed on its side, next to a lemon half with a small label that says 0.9 V.

terms.meaning: One of the two ends of a cell where a wire is joined. Electrons leave from the minus terminal and return to the plus terminal.
terms.example: On an AA cell the flat end is the minus terminal. The end with the bump is the plus terminal.
terms.art: An AA cell with a minus sign at its flat end and a plus sign at its bumped end.

terms.meaning: A list of metals in order. At the top are the metals that give away electrons most easily. At the bottom are those that hold them most strongly. Scientists call it the activity series.
terms.example: Zinc is above copper on the ladder. So in a lemon cell the zinc gives the electrons.
terms.art: A ladder with eight rungs labelled from top to bottom: magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, tin, copper, silver, gold.

terms.meaning: Using an electric current to force a chemical change that would not happen alone.
terms.example: A current from four AA cells splits water into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas.
terms.art: A glass of water with two pencils in it joined to a pack of four cells, and streams of small bubbles rising from both pencil tips.

terms.meaning: The slow change of a metal into another substance as it gives away electrons, usually to oxygen.
terms.example: A green crust on an old copper pot and rust on a gate are both corrosion.
terms.art: An old copper pot with a green crust on one side and a rusty iron hinge beside it.

terms.meaning: The flaky orange-brown substance that forms when iron corrodes. It is made of iron, oxygen and water joined together.
terms.example: A cycle chain left out in the monsoon is covered in rust within a week.
terms.art: A close view of a bicycle chain covered in orange-brown flaky rust.

terms.meaning: Coated with a thin layer of zinc. The zinc corrodes in place of the iron under it.
terms.example: A galvanised bucket stays grey for years where a plain iron bucket would rust.
terms.art: A dull grey galvanised bucket standing next to a plain iron bucket covered in rust.

terms.meaning: A cell that joins hydrogen and oxygen into water and gives an electric current as it does so. It is electrolysis of water run backwards.
terms.example: Some buses run on fuel cells. Only water comes out of their exhaust pipes.
terms.art: A bus with a tank marked H2 on its roof and drops of water falling from its exhaust pipe.

explanations.concept: Metals hold some of their electrons loosely
explanations.definition: An electron is a tiny particle with a minus charge, and every atom has electrons. An ion is an atom that has lost or gained electrons.
explanations.description: Everything is made of atoms, and every atom has electrons. In a metal, each atom holds its outermost electrons loosely. These loose electrons can move from atom to atom through the whole piece. That is why metals carry electricity. A metal atom can also give its loose electrons away completely. Then it is no longer an atom of metal. It has become an ion, and an ion behaves very differently. A zinc atom sits firmly in a solid nail. A zinc ion can leave the nail and float away in juice or water. So when a metal gives away electrons, the metal is slowly used up. Some metals give electrons away easily, and others hold on to them strongly. Batteries, electrolysis and rust all follow from that difference.
examples: A copper wire carries a current because its loose electrons can move along it.
A zinc nail in lemon juice slowly loses zinc, because zinc atoms become ions and float away.
A gold ring stays bright for centuries, because gold atoms hold their electrons strongly.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in piece of metal drawn as rows of balls with small dots moving freely between them, and one ball at the edge drifting away into a liquid.

explanations.concept: A lemon cell: two different metals and a liquid with ions
explanations.definition: A cell is two different metals, or other substances, with an electrolyte between them. A chemical change in the cell pushes electrons round a wire.
explanations.description: Zinc gives away electrons more easily than copper does. In a lemon cell, zinc atoms leave their electrons behind in the nail. The atoms go into the juice as zinc ions. The electrons left behind crowd the nail, so the nail is the minus terminal. A wire gives them a path to the copper, and they flow along it. At the copper, the electrons are taken by hydrogen ions from the acid in the juice. These become tiny bubbles of hydrogen gas. The copper itself does not change. Inside the lemon, ions drift through the juice and complete the loop. The energy of the current comes from the zinc as it changes. The lemon only supplies the juice, which carries the ions and holds the acid. When the zinc is used up, the cell is dead.
examples: A zinc nail and a copper wire in a lemon give about 0.9 volts.
Two copper wires in a lemon give nothing, because neither one gives electrons more easily than the other.
The same two metals work in a potato, in vinegar or in salt water.
explanations.art: A cut-away lemon with a zinc nail on the left and a copper wire on the right, arrows showing electrons going from the nail through an outside wire to the copper, and small grey ions drifting from the nail into the juice.

explanations.concept: The metal ladder: why the two metals must be different
explanations.definition: The metal ladder, or activity series, is a list of metals in order. It runs from those that give away electrons most easily to those that hold them most strongly.
explanations.description: Chemists have tested metals against each other and put them in order. From the top, eight common ones are magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, tin, copper, silver and gold. When two metals share an electrolyte, the one higher on the ladder gives electrons to the lower one. The further apart they are on the ladder, the harder the push, and the more volts the cell gives. Two pieces of the same metal sit on the same rung, so there is no push at all. The ladder also explains where metals are found. Gold is at the bottom and holds its electrons strongly, so it lies in the ground as shiny metal. Iron is higher, so in the ground it is always joined to oxygen as ore. Aluminium is near the top, but a thin, hard skin of aluminium oxide covers it. That skin is why foil often acts as if aluminium were lower on the ladder.
examples: Zinc and copper are three rungs apart, and they make a good cell.
Copper and copper are on the same rung, and they make no cell.
Gold is found as nuggets. Iron is found only as ore.
explanations.art: A ladder with eight metals written on its rungs, an arrow pointing down beside it labelled 'electrons go this way', and a zinc nail and a copper wire drawn at their rungs.

explanations.concept: Volts say how hard a cell pushes, not how much it can give
explanations.definition: A volt is the unit for how hard a cell pushes electrons. The number of electrons that pass each second is called the current.
explanations.description: A lemon cell pushes with about 0.9 volts, and an AA cell with 1.5 volts. Cells joined in a row, plus to minus, add their pushes. Four lemon cells give about 3.6 volts, which is more than two AA cells. Yet four lemons light only a small red LED, and only faintly. They can never light a torch bulb. The reason is that a lemon cell lets very few electrons through each second. Its ions drift slowly through the juice, and the metals touch only a little juice. A torch bulb needs hundreds of times more electrons each second than a lemon can pass. An AA cell is built to pass that many. So a battery has two different numbers: how hard it pushes, and how much it can deliver. A wall socket pushes with 230 volts and can deliver enough to kill. That is why this unit uses only small cells.
examples: One lemon cell gives about 0.9 volts. Four lemon cells joined in a row give about 3.6 volts.
A red LED needs about 1.8 volts and very few electrons each second, so lemons can light it.
A torch bulb needs many electrons each second, so lemons cannot light it.
explanations.art: Four lemon halves in a row lighting a tiny red LED faintly, and beside them one AA cell lighting a torch bulb brightly.

explanations.definition: A shop cell works like a lemon cell. One substance gives electrons, another takes them, and a paste with ions lies between them.
explanations.description: In a common AA cell, the giver of electrons is zinc, just as in the lemon. In the cheapest kind, called zinc-carbon, the outer can is the zinc. Inside is a black paste that holds manganese dioxide, which takes the electrons. A carbon rod down the middle collects them. As the cell works, the zinc can is eaten away. That is why very old cells leak, and why cells should be taken out of toys that are put away. An alkaline cell uses zinc powder and lasts longer. A phone battery is a different kind, called lithium-ion. In it, lithium ions move from one layered material to another, and charging pushes them back. Button cells need special care. If a small child swallows one, the current makes a strong base in the wet food pipe within two hours. This burns badly. Keep button cells out of reach, and go to hospital at once if one is swallowed.
examples: A zinc-carbon AA cell: the zinc can gives electrons, and manganese dioxide takes them.
An old cell left in a toy leaks, because its zinc can has been eaten through.
A phone battery can be charged, because the change inside it can be pushed backwards.
explanations.art: An AA cell cut in half lengthwise, showing a thin zinc can on the outside, black paste inside and a dark carbon rod down the middle.

explanations.concept: Electrolysis: a current forces a change, and splits water
explanations.definition: Electrolysis is using an electric current to force a chemical change. In the electrolysis of water, the current splits water into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas.
explanations.description: A water molecule is two hydrogen atoms joined to one oxygen atom. The atoms hold on to each other strongly, and boiling does not separate them. A current can. Two electrodes joined to a pack of cells dip into water with a little baking soda in it. The soda gives the water ions, so that it can carry a current. The cells push electrons into the minus electrode. Water molecules there take the electrons and break up, and hydrogen gas bubbles off. What is left behind there turns the water into a base, which is the opposite of an acid. The cells pull electrons out of the plus electrode. Water molecules there give up electrons, and oxygen gas bubbles off. Twice as much hydrogen comes off as oxygen, because water has two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom. A battery gives energy as its change runs. Electrolysis uses energy to push a change the other way. Charging a phone is electrolysis inside its battery.
examples: Two pencil leads joined to four AA cells bubble in baking soda water.
A space station splits water by electrolysis to make oxygen for the crew to breathe.
A phone charger pushes the change inside the phone's battery backwards.
explanations.art: A glass of water with two pencil leads joined to a pack of cells, many bubbles labelled hydrogen at the minus lead and half as many labelled oxygen at the plus lead.

explanations.definition: Rust is the flaky orange-brown substance that forms when iron gives electrons to oxygen while water is present.
explanations.description: A drop of water on a steel plate sets up a tiny cell. Steel is iron with a little carbon in it. Under the middle of the drop, iron atoms give away electrons and go into the water as iron ions. The electrons travel through the steel to the edge of the drop. More oxygen reaches the water there from the air. There the oxygen and water take the electrons. The iron ions meet what the oxygen has made, and together they form rust. So rusting needs three things at once: iron, water and oxygen. Dry iron hardly rusts, and iron deep under still water with no air hardly rusts. Salt speeds rusting, because salty water carries ions well. That is why cycles, grills and cars rust fastest near the sea. Rust is flaky and lets water through, so the iron below keeps rusting. Aluminium corrodes too, but its oxide forms a tight skin that seals the metal.
examples: A steel kadai left wet overnight has orange spots by morning.
A window grill in Chennai or Kochi rusts faster than one in Jaipur, because sea air is damp and salty.
An iron nail kept in a dry tin stays grey for years.
explanations.art: A water drop on a steel plate seen from the side, with a small pit under the middle of the drop, arrows through the metal to the edge of the drop, and a ring of orange rust near the edge.

explanations.definition: Rust is stopped by keeping water and oxygen off the iron. It is also stopped by giving the iron electrons from elsewhere, or by changing the iron.
explanations.description: The first way is a coat. Paint, oil, grease and plastic keep water and air off the iron. A scratch in the coat lets rust start. The second way is a bodyguard metal from higher on the metal ladder. A galvanised bucket has a coat of zinc. Zinc gives away electrons more easily than iron, so the zinc corrodes and the iron is spared. This works even at a scratch, as long as the zinc touches the iron. Steel ships and fishing boats carry blocks of zinc bolted to the hull for the same reason. The third way is to push electrons into the iron from a power supply. Long buried pipelines for gas and oil are protected like this. The fourth way is to change the metal. Stainless steel is iron with chromium added. The chromium forms a thin, tight skin of oxide that you cannot see, and it mends itself when scratched.
examples: Railings are painted again every few years to keep water off the iron.
Tin roofing sheets are galvanised steel, and last for decades in the rain.
A stainless steel tumbler holds water every day and does not rust.
explanations.art: Four small pictures: a painted gate, a galvanised bucket, a buried pipe joined by a wire to a box, and a shiny steel tumbler.

explanations.concept: Living bodies move ions and pass electrons too
explanations.definition: Living cells work by moving ions across their walls and by passing electrons from food to oxygen.
explanations.description: Every nerve and muscle cell in humans and other animals pumps ions across the cell wall. This makes a difference of less than a tenth of a volt between the inside and the outside. A nerve signal is that difference changing, step by step, along the nerve. An electric eel has thousands of flat cells stacked in rows, like lemon cells joined in a row. Their small pushes add up. In 2019 scientists measured 860 volts from one kind of electric eel, and named that kind after Alessandro Volta. Electrons matter to every living being in another way. Your cells take electrons from the food you eat and pass them, in small steps, to the oxygen you breathe. The energy you live on comes from that passing. Some bacteria who live in mud with no air pass their electrons to rust in place of oxygen. They live by using rust the way we use air.
examples: A nerve cell holds a difference of about 0.07 volts across its wall.
An electric eel stacks thousands of cells in a row to stun a fish.
Bacteria called Geobacter pass electrons to rust in mud where there is no air.
explanations.art: An electric eel in brown river water, with a small inset showing rows of flat cells stacked like coins along the eel's body.

explanations.concept: Rust, water and electrons on the Earth and in space
explanations.definition: The same passing of electrons shapes rocks, planets and spacecraft.
explanations.description: Iron ore is mostly iron joined to oxygen, which is the same kind of substance as rust. A steel plant uses great heat and carbon to pull the oxygen away and leave iron. Rusting puts the oxygen back. So a rusting gate is slowly going back to what it was in the ground. Mars looks red because its dust is full of iron oxides. On the International Space Station, a machine splits water by electrolysis to give the crew oxygen. The Apollo spacecraft that flew to the Moon carried fuel cells. These joined hydrogen and oxygen, gave electric current, and made water that the crew drank. On Earth, engineers now build large electrolysers that run on sunlight and wind. The hydrogen they make can be stored and used later as a fuel.
examples: The red hills of iron ore at Ballari in Karnataka and in Odisha are iron joined to oxygen.
Mars is called the red planet because of iron oxide dust.
The space station makes oxygen for breathing by splitting water.
explanations.art: A red hill of iron ore on the left, a rusty gate in the middle and the red planet Mars on the right, joined by a thin orange line.

explanations.concept: What will store the world's electricity?
explanations.definition: Sunlight and wind do not give power at every hour, so the electricity must be stored. Engineers disagree about the best way.
explanations.description: Solar panels make most of their electricity at midday, and people need most of it in the evening. Something must hold the energy in between. Each way of storing it has gains and costs, and working engineers back different ones.
examples: A phone stores energy in a lithium-ion battery.
A hydrogen plant stores energy by splitting water.

perspectives.explanation: They give back about nine tenths of the energy put in, and they get cheaper every year. But lithium and cobalt must be mined, and that harms land and people.
Sodium comes from common salt, so it is cheap and found everywhere. These batteries are heavier for the energy they hold, and they are still new.
Hydrogen made by splitting water can be stored for months and can run ships and steel plants. But more than half the energy is lost on the way there and back.

explanations.art: A solar panel at midday with three arrows leading to a battery, a pile of salt and a tank marked H2.

explanations.concept: Did life begin at a natural battery?
explanations.definition: One idea is that life began at vents on the deep sea floor. There, rocks and sea water made a natural electrical difference.
explanations.description: On the deep sea floor there are vents where warm water full of minerals seeps out of the rock. The vent water is a base, and the early sea was slightly acid. Thin walls of minerals with iron and sulfur in them stood between the two. Some scientists think this made a natural difference, like the two sides of a cell. On this idea, the first living things used that difference for energy. Every cell still uses a difference across its wall today. Nobody has shown that life began this way. It is one idea among several.
examples: Warm, mineral-rich vents of this kind were found on the Atlantic sea floor in the year 2000.

perspectives.who: Scientists who favour deep-sea vents, such as Michael Russell and Nick Lane
perspectives.explanation: Every living cell runs on a difference of ions across its wall. A vent offers that difference ready-made, so life may have started there.

perspectives.who: Scientists who favour warm ponds on land
perspectives.explanation: The building blocks of life join up best when they dry out and get wet again. That happens in ponds on land, and it does not happen on the sea floor.

explanations.art: A pale chimney of rock on the dark sea floor with warm water rising from it, and a zoomed-in circle showing a thin mineral wall with plus signs on one side.

agreed.text: A battery gives a current because a chemical change inside it moves electrons from one substance to another.
agreed.evidence: In the 1830s Michael Faraday measured how much zinc a cell lost. The amount of electricity always matched the amount of zinc used up.

agreed.text: Two electrodes of the same metal in the same liquid give no current.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can check this. Two copper wires in a lemon give no reading on a meter and no crackle in earphones.

agreed.text: An electric current splits water into two parts of hydrogen gas and one part of oxygen gas.
agreed.evidence: William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle first did this in London in May 1800. Every careful measurement since has given two to one.

agreed.text: Iron rusts only where water and oxygen are both present.
agreed.evidence: A nail in dry air stays grey. A nail in boiled water under a layer of oil stays grey. A nail in open water rusts.

agreed.text: Rusting is a passing of electrons, like the change in a cell. The iron is eaten at one place and the oxygen takes electrons at another.
agreed.evidence: In the 1920s Ulick Evans in Cambridge put drops of salt water on steel. The steel was eaten under the middle of each drop, and the oxygen took electrons at the edge.

agreed.text: A metal higher on the metal ladder protects a lower one that it touches.
agreed.evidence: Galvanised steel stays free of rust at a scratch. Zinc blocks on ships are eaten away while the steel hull beside them is not.

challenging.claim: A lemon battery gets its electricity from the lemon.
challenging.who: Many books and videos call the lemon the source of power.
challenging.for: Without the lemon nothing happens, and a dry, old lemon works badly.
challenging.against: Two wires of the same metal in a lemon give nothing. The metals work just as well in salt water. The zinc is used up, and the lemon is only the path.

challenging.claim: People made batteries in Iraq about 2,000 years ago.
challenging.who: Wilhelm König, who worked at the national museum in Baghdad, suggested this in 1938.
challenging.for: A clay jar found near Baghdad held a copper tube with an iron rod inside. Copies filled with vinegar give a small voltage.
challenging.against: No wires were found with the jar, and no object that the current could have been used on. Similar jars held rolled-up writings. Most archaeologists think this one was for storage.

challenging.who: The name says so, and most people believe it.
challenging.for: A stainless steel tumbler holds water for years and stays bright.
challenging.against: The thin skin of chromium oxide can break down in salty water or sea air. Brown spots and small pits then form. Stainless steel resists rust well, but it can still rust.

challenging.claim: The Iron Pillar of Delhi has hardly rusted in 1,600 years because of what its iron is made of.
challenging.who: The metal scientist R. Balasubramaniam of IIT Kanpur, in studies published around the year 2000.
challenging.for: The iron holds much more phosphorus than modern steel. He showed that this helps a thin, tight layer to form on the surface. The layer keeps water off the iron below.
challenging.against: An older view is that Delhi's dry air is the main reason. Both probably help. The part of the pillar below the ground has rusted more.

challenging.claim: Hydrogen made by splitting water will replace petrol and diesel.
challenging.who: Many governments and companies. India began a National Green Hydrogen Mission in 2023.
challenging.for: Hydrogen can be made from water with sunlight, and using it gives back only water.
challenging.against: Splitting water takes more energy than the hydrogen gives back. Hydrogen is hard to store. For cars, batteries waste much less energy. Hydrogen may suit ships, steel plants and fertiliser factories better.

big_questions.q: The lemon had no electricity in it. So where was the energy before the earphones crackled?
big_questions.hint: Zinc is found in the ground joined to other things. A factory used energy to make it into metal.

big_questions.q: Rusting passes electrons, just as a battery does. Is a rusting gate a battery that nobody has joined to a wire?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the energy of a rusting gate goes.

big_questions.q: Iron comes out of the ground as a kind of rust, and it goes back to rust. Is a steel bridge ever finished?
big_questions.hint: Think about how often a railing is painted, and what happens if nobody paints it.

big_questions.q: You breathe oxygen so that it can take electrons from your food. Iron rusts when oxygen takes its electrons. Are you rusting?
big_questions.hint: Both pass electrons to oxygen. A body does it in small steps and uses the energy.

big_questions.q: Mars is red with iron oxide. What might that tell us about the past of Mars?
big_questions.hint: On Earth, iron rusts where there is water and oxygen.

big_questions.q: The metals in a phone battery are dug up by miners, some of whom are children. Who should pay the real cost of a battery?
big_questions.hint: Think about who digs up the metals, who buys the phones, and who gains from each. Much of the world's cobalt comes from mines in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

story.title: The Grey Lumps Under the Boat
story.note: Jenifer, Stella Periyamma, Xavier Mama and the two boats are made up, and so are the weights and the price. These facts are real. Fishing boats on India's east coast stay out of the sea for about two months from mid-April. Steel boats with bronze propellers carry blocks of zinc bolted to the hull. The zinc is eaten away and is replaced when the boat is hauled out. A zinc block must touch bare metal and must never be painted.
text: Every April, when the fishing ban began, the trawler Kadal Rani came out of the sea. A winch pulled the boat up the slipway at Thoothukudi harbour, dripping, and for two months no net went into the water.

Jenifer was nine, and this year her aunt had given her a scraper. Stella Periyamma repaired boats. She could weld a split steel plate in the time it took the tea boy to cross the yard. Her rule for helpers was short. "Scrape first. Ask afterwards."

So Jenifer scraped. Barnacle shells came off the steel hull in grey crusts, and under them the red paint was whole. She worked her way along to the stern, where the bronze propeller hung, as yellow as a temple lamp.
Beside the propeller, two grey lumps were bolted to the hull. They were ugly. They were pitted like pumice stone and crusted with white, and one corner crumbled when she pushed it with the scraper.
"Periyamma! These two are rotten."
"They are," said her aunt, without looking up from her welding.
"The paint is fine. The propeller is fine. Only these are eaten."
"Take them off, then." A spanner slid across the concrete.

It took Jenifer a long time to turn the bolts. When the lumps came away, she carried them to the hanging scale by the store room, because her aunt weighed everything. Each lump weighed one kilogram. In the store room was a box of new ones. They were smooth and silver-grey, as neat as bars of soap. She weighed one of those too. Three kilograms.
She did the sum standing there. In one year, something had eaten two whole kilograms of metal off each lump.
"It is bad metal," she told her aunt. "The sea eats it. We should bolt on something strong. Steel. Or bronze, like the propeller. The sea has not touched the propeller."
"Hm," said Stella Periyamma. She pushed up her mask. "Take this tea to Xavier Mama on the next slipway. Look at his rudder while you are there. Then come and tell me again what to bolt on."
The next boat was called Annai. Xavier Mama stood under the stern with his hands on his hips. He took the tea and did not drink it.

The rudder of Annai was a sorry sight. The steel was full of pits, some as deep as Jenifer's fingertip. Along one edge there were holes right through it, and she could see daylight in them, as in a dosa. The heads of the bolts were worn thin and sharp.

"Last year I saved eight hundred rupees," said Xavier Mama. "I told your aunt: why should I pay every year for lumps that only rot? Leave them off." He tapped the rudder, and brown flakes fell on his foot. "Now I am buying a rudder."
Jenifer looked along the hull. Near the propeller there were four bolt holes with nothing bolted to them. The bronze propeller shone, without a mark on it.
She walked back slowly. Two boats had sat in the same sea for the same year. On one boat the lumps were eaten and the steel was whole. On the other there were no lumps, and the steel was eaten.
"The sea was going to eat something," she said to her aunt. "On our boat it ate the lumps. On his boat there were no lumps, so it ate the rudder."
"Go on."
"So the lumps are not bad metal. They are there to be eaten."

Stella Periyamma put down her torch. "They are zinc. Steel, bronze and zinc all sit in the same salt water, and all are bolted together. When metals touch like that, they do not corrode equally. One of them gives up its electrons first, and that one is eaten. The others are left alone for as long as it lasts. Zinc gives up electrons more easily than steel. Steel gives them up more easily than bronze."
Jenifer thought of the propeller on Annai, bright and whole beside the ruined rudder. "So on his boat the steel was the one."
"On his boat the steel did the zinc's job."
Jenifer fetched two new blocks from the box. Then she had an idea, and fetched the tin of red paint as well. "If I paint them," she said, "they will last two years."

Her aunt took the brush out of her hand, gently. "Paint the zinc, and the sea cannot reach it. Then it protects nothing, and the rudder goes." She scrubbed the hull around the bolt holes with a wire brush until the steel showed bright. "No paint under it either. Metal must touch metal, or the electrons have no road."
They bolted the blocks on to the bare steel, and Jenifer was allowed the last turn of the spanner on each. The new zinc looked too clean for a boat.
"Next April they will be ugly again," she said.
"I hope so," said Stella Periyamma. "The year they come up clean is the year I worry."

In June the ban ended. The winch let Kadal Rani down the slipway, and the water closed over the propeller and the two grey blocks. Jenifer watched until she could not see them. Nobody would look at them again for ten months, and they had already begun to be eaten.
story.epiphany: Two boats sat in the same sea. The boat with zinc blocks lost zinc and kept its steel. The boat without zinc lost its steel. When different metals touch in salt water, the one that gives up electrons most easily is eaten. The others are spared.
ask: The bronze propeller was unmarked on both boats. Why did the sea leave it alone?
Why would a coat of paint on the zinc block stop it protecting the steel?
Where in your home or street is zinc doing this job for iron?
