games.title: Battery, Electrolysis or Corrosion? A sorting card game
games.context: This is a card game about three ways electrons pass from one substance to another. Each card describes something real, and you say which of the three it is.

setup.art: Eighteen cards in a shuffled pile on a table, with three small tokens marked Battery, Electrolysis and Corrosion in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One player reading a card aloud while another slides one token forward, face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads the front. Everyone else puts down one token, face down.

setup.art: The tokens turned face up and the reader showing the back of the card.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader reads the back.

printables.title: 18 cards: something that happens on the front, its kind and the reason on the back

items.f: Two AAA cells make a TV remote work.
items.b: Battery. A chemical change inside the cells pushes electrons through the remote.

items.f: A zinc nail and a copper wire in a lemon make earphones crackle.
items.b: Battery. The zinc gives away electrons, and they flow through the earphones to the copper.

items.f: An electric eel stuns a fish with a shock.
items.b: Battery. Thousands of flat cells in the eel's body are stacked in a row, and their pushes add up.

items.f: A phone plays a film while it is not plugged in.
items.b: Battery. The change inside the phone's battery pushes electrons through the phone.

items.f: A tiny button cell in a hearing aid uses zinc and the oxygen in air.
items.b: Battery. The zinc gives electrons and the oxygen takes them, and the current runs the hearing aid.

items.f: A bus joins hydrogen from a tank with oxygen from the air, and its motor turns.
items.b: Battery. This is a fuel cell. Hydrogen gives electrons, and they pass through the motor to the oxygen.

items.f: A phone is plugged in and its battery fills up.
items.b: Electrolysis. The charger's current pushes the change in the battery backwards.

items.f: A machine on the space station turns water into oxygen for the crew.
items.b: Electrolysis. A current from the solar panels splits water into hydrogen and oxygen.

items.f: A factory passes a huge current through melted ore and collects aluminium metal.
items.b: Electrolysis. The current forces electrons back on to aluminium ions, and metal forms.

items.f: A steel spoon in a bath of silver solution, joined to a power supply, gets a silver coat.
items.b: Electrolysis. The current forces silver ions to take electrons and settle on the spoon as metal.

items.f: Two pencils joined to four AA cells bubble in baking soda water.
items.b: Electrolysis. The current splits water. Hydrogen comes off one pencil and oxygen off the other.

items.f: A car's engine runs and fills up the car's battery again.
items.b: Electrolysis. A current from the engine's generator pushes the battery's change backwards.

items.f: An iron gate turns orange-brown after the monsoon.
items.b: Corrosion. The iron gives electrons to oxygen, with rainwater present, and rust forms.

items.f: An old copper pot grows a green crust.
items.b: Corrosion. The copper slowly gives electrons to oxygen and joins with things in the air and water.

items.f: A silver anklet turns dark in a drawer.
items.b: Corrosion. The silver gives electrons to sulfur in the air and forms a dark layer.

items.f: A cycle chain left in the rain turns stiff and brown.
items.b: Corrosion. The steel gives electrons to oxygen in the rainwater, and rust forms between the links.

items.f: A zinc block bolted to a steel boat is slowly eaten away in the sea.
items.b: Corrosion. The zinc gives electrons in place of the steel. People fix it there on purpose.

items.f: The aluminium frame around a steel bolt turns white and pitted near the sea.
items.b: Corrosion. Aluminium is above iron on the metal ladder, so the aluminium gives the electrons.

printables.title: 3 answer tokens: Battery, Electrolysis, Corrosion. Print one set for each player

rules: A battery is a chemical change that pushes electrons through a wire. Electrolysis is a current that forces a chemical change. Corrosion is a metal giving electrons away with no wire.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one token face down. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches scores 1 point.
A player who also names what gives the electrons, or what forces the change, scores 1 more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
With two players, swap the reader's role after every card. Playing alone? Read a card, say your answer aloud, then turn the card over.
After all 18 cards, the player with the most points wins. If you play alone, your score out of 18 is your result.

flow.do: Cut out the 18 cards and the tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player one set of three tokens. Read the first rule aloud.
flow.say: A battery is a chemical change that makes a current. Electrolysis is a current that forces a chemical change. Corrosion is a metal giving electrons away with no wire at all.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take three tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Battery, Electrolysis or Corrosion. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first nine cards. After each card, read the back aloud. Ask the question below after card five.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and put it face down. Now turn it over. The reader reads the back. Who scored?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: How do you tell a battery from electrolysis?
good: In a battery the change makes the current.
In electrolysis the current comes from outside and forces the change.
I ask whether something is plugged in or being charged.

flow.parent: A useful question for a stuck child is: does the current come out of this, or go into it?
flow.context: In this step of Battery, Electrolysis or Corrosion you play the first nine cards.

flow.do: Play the last nine cards the same way. Keep the score on a piece of paper.
flow.say: Nine more cards. This time, also say what gives away the electrons. A right answer earns one more point.
flow.kid: Play nine more cards. Say what gives away the electrons.
flow.context: In this step of Battery, Electrolysis or Corrosion you play the last nine cards and name what gives the electrons.

flow.do: Count the points. Then sort all 18 cards into three piles and look at the piles.
flow.say: Sort the cards into three piles. In which pile do the electrons do useful work on the way? In which pile is their energy lost as a little heat?
flow.kid: Sort the cards into three piles. Where do electrons do useful work?

check.q: A rusting gate and a torch cell both pass electrons from a metal. What is the main difference?
options: In the cell, the electrons go through a wire
Rust uses bigger electrons
A cell has no metal in it
check.why: In both, a metal gives away electrons. In a cell, the electrons must travel through a wire to reach what takes them. So they can light a bulb on the way. In rusting they pass straight through the iron, and the energy becomes a little heat.

flow.context: This is the last step of Battery, Electrolysis or Corrosion. You sort the cards into three piles and compare them.

games.title: Volt Makers: a metal ladder card game
games.context: This is a card game about the metal ladder. You pair two metals to make a cell, and the pair that is furthest apart on the ladder scores most.

setup.art: A printed strip showing a ladder of eight metals numbered 1 to 8, lying in the middle of a table.
setup.caption: 1. Put the metal ladder where everyone can see it.

setup.art: Two players each holding four metal cards, with a pile of cards face down between them.
setup.caption: 2. Deal four cards to each player. Put the rest in a pile.

setup.art: A player laying down a Zinc card and a Copper card side by side and pointing at the ladder.
setup.caption: 3. Lay down two cards as a cell. Count the rungs between them.

printables.title: 1 metal ladder: eight metals in order, from the easiest giver of electrons to the strongest holder
items: Rung 1: Magnesium. Burns with a bright white light.
Rung 2: Aluminium. It is used for kitchen foil, and a thin skin of oxide protects it.
Rung 3: Zinc. It makes the coat on a galvanised bucket.
Rung 4: Iron. Steel is mostly iron.
Rung 5: Tin. It makes the thin coat inside a food tin.
Rung 6: Copper. It is used for electric wires.
Rung 7: Silver. It is used for anklets and old coins.
Rung 8: Gold. Found in the ground as shiny metal.

printables.title: 24 metal cards: three of each metal, with its rung on the ladder

rules: Put the ladder in the middle. Shuffle the 24 cards. Deal four cards to each player, and put the rest face down in a pile.
On your turn, lay down two cards from your hand, side by side. They are the two metals of a cell.
Say which of the two metals gives the electrons. It is the one higher on the ladder, with the smaller rung number.
If you are right, score the number of rungs between the two metals. Zinc and copper score 3. Two cards of the same metal score 0.
Take two new cards from the pile, if any are left. Then the next player has a turn.
The game ends when the pile is empty and every card has been laid down. The player with the most points wins.
Playing alone? Deal yourself four cards and play through the whole pack. A total of 36 or more is a very good score. The most anyone can get is 48.

flow.do: Cut out the ladder and the 24 cards. Shuffle and deal four cards to each player. Read the rules aloud.
flow.say: Two metals in a cell push harder when they are far apart on the ladder. Two of the same metal do not push at all. Which pair on the ladder do you think is best?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Deal four each. Which two metals are furthest apart?
flow.context: This is the first step of Volt Makers. You set up the metal ladder and deal the cards.

flow.do: Play until the pile is empty and all the cards are laid down. Each player says which metal gives the electrons before they score. Keep the score on paper.
flow.say: Lay down two metals. Which one gives the electrons? How many rungs apart are they? Is it better to use your gold now, or keep it for a magnesium?
flow.kid: Lay down two cards. Say which metal gives electrons. Count the rungs.

ask.q: Why do two copper cards score nothing?
good: They are on the same rung, so neither gives electrons to the other.
Two copper wires in a lemon gave no crackle.

flow.parent: The rungs give the right order of real cells, but not their exact volts. Real zinc and copper give about 1 volt.
flow.context: In this step of Volt Makers you pair metal cards into cells and score the rungs between them.

flow.do: Add up the scores. Then ask the question below.
flow.say: Who scored most? Which pair was the best cell in the whole game? In that pair, which metal would be used up?
flow.kid: Add up the points. Which pair was best? Which metal gets used up?

check.q: In a cell made of iron and silver, which metal gives away electrons and is used up?
options: The iron, which is higher on the ladder
The silver, which is shinier
Both, at the same speed
check.why: The metal higher on the ladder gives away electrons more easily. Iron is on rung 4 and silver is on rung 7. So the iron gives the electrons and is slowly used up, and the silver is unchanged.

flow.context: This is the last step of Volt Makers. You add up the scores and say which metal in a pair is used up.

experiments.title: The Lemon Battery: which pairs of metals make a lemon crackle?
experiments.question: Earphones crackle when electrons flow through them. Which makes them crackle: two copper wires in a lemon, two zinc nails in a lemon, or one of each? What happens with two lemon cells in a row?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which pair will make the earphones crackle: copper and copper, zinc and zinc, or copper and zinc? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same lemon half for the three pairs. Push every piece in 2 centimetres deep, and keep the two pieces 2 centimetres apart. Use the same earphones and the same listener, in a quiet room. Wipe the plug dry between tests. Only the pair of metals changes.

materials.item: juicy lemons

galvanised nails about 5 centimetres long. A galvanised nail is a steel nail with a coat of zinc, and this unit calls it a zinc nail. If you have none, fold four strips of kitchen foil, each 8 centimetres by 6, three times lengthwise
pieces of bare copper wire, each 10 centimetres long. A grown-up strips the plastic off an old piece of electric wire that is not joined to anything
wired earphones with a round plug. Wireless earphones and earphones with a flat plug do not work for this
small plates or steel lids, one for each lemon half
a red LED, if you have one
a knife for the grown-up, a dry cloth, a pencil and a notebook page for the results

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the lemons and strips the wire. The nails are sharp. Do not eat the lemons afterwards, because zinc and copper have gone into the juice. Wash your hands at the end.

schedule.what: Test the three pairs of metals, then two cells and four cells in a row.
Pull the zinc nail and the copper wire out of the lemon and compare them.

experiments.record: Draw a table with six rows, one for each test. The first three rows are copper and copper, zinc and zinc, and copper and zinc. The last three are two cells in a row, two cells facing each other, and four cells in a row. Beside each, write 'none', 'faint' or 'loud'.
experiments.context: In this experiment you push pairs of metals into a lemon and listen with earphones. You find out which pairs make electrons flow.

setup.art: Two lemons cut in half, each half sitting cut side up on its own small steel lid, with four grey nails and four copper wires beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut two lemons in half. Put each half on its own lid.

setup.art: One lemon half with two pieces pushed into its cut face, 2 centimetres apart: a grey nail and a copper wire.
setup.caption: 2. Push two pieces of metal into one half, 2 centimetres apart.

setup.art: A hand pressing the end of the copper wire against the metal band next to the tip of an earphone plug, while the tip of the plug scrapes the head of the nail.
setup.caption: 3. Press the wire on the band next to the plug's tip. Scrape the tip on the other metal.

setup.art: Two lemon halves side by side, the copper wire of the first twisted round the nail of the second.
setup.caption: 4. Join two cells in a row: the copper of one to the zinc of the next.

setup.art: A grey nail pulled out of a lemon the next day, its lower half dark and rough and its upper half still shiny, next to a bright copper wire.
setup.caption: 5. The next day, compare the zinc nail with the copper wire.

flow.do: Lay out the lemons, the zinc nails, the copper wires and the earphones. Touch the plug to a whole lemon so your child hears that nothing happens. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Earphones crackle when electrons flow through them. A lemon alone gives no crackle. We will push two pieces of metal into the lemon. Which pair will make a crackle: two copper wires, two zinc nails, or one of each? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the copper wires and zinc nails. Which pair will make a crackle? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that pair will work?
good: Two different metals might behave differently.
Copper is used in wires, so two coppers should be best.
Any metal will do, because the lemon has the power.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children, and many adults, expect the lemon to be the source of the electricity.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Lemon Battery test. You guess which pair of metals will make earphones crackle.

flow.do: Roll each lemon hard on the table to loosen the juice. Cut both in half. Put each half, cut side up, on its own lid. Strip four pieces of copper wire, 10 centimetres each, and twist the thin strands of each together.
flow.say: Each lemon half sits on its own lid, so that no juice joins one half to another. These nails are steel with a coat of zinc. We will call them zinc nails.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the lemons and strips the wire. Put each half on a lid.
flow.parent: Use only wire that is not joined to anything. If you use foil strips in place of zinc nails, the crackles are a little fainter.
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Battery test a grown-up cuts two lemons and prepares four copper wires.

flow.do: Push two copper wires 2 centimetres deep into one lemon half, 2 centimetres apart. Put the earbuds in your child's ears. Press the end of one wire on the metal band next to the plug's tip. Scrape the tip on the other wire. Record the result. Then do the same with two zinc nails.
flow.say: Two copper wires are in the lemon. Hold one wire on the band next to the tip of the plug. Now scrape the tip on the other wire. What do you hear? Now we try two zinc nails.
flow.kid: Put two copper wires in the lemon. Scrape the plug on one. Listen. Then try two zinc nails.
flow.parent: Expect silence both times. A very faint tick can happen if one piece is dirtier than the other. Wipe both with the dry cloth and try again.
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Battery test you listen to a lemon holding two pieces of the same metal.

flow.do: Leave one copper wire in the lemon half. Push one zinc nail in, 2 centimetres from it. Press the copper wire on the band next to the tip. Scrape the tip on the head of the nail. Record the result.
flow.say: Now the lemon holds one copper wire and one zinc nail. Scrape the tip of the plug on the nail. What do you hear this time?
flow.kid: Now use one copper wire and one zinc nail. Scrape the plug on the nail. Listen.

check.q: Two copper wires gave no crackle. One copper wire and one zinc nail gave a crackle. What does that show?
options: The two metals must be different
Copper is a poor metal for wires
The lemon had run out of juice
check.why: The lemon and the earphones were the same each time. Only the pair of metals changed, so the difference between the metals makes the electrons flow. If you chose 'the lemon ran out of juice', remember that the same lemon crackled a minute later.

flow.parent: The crackle comes each time the tip touches the nail or leaves it. This is one lemon cell. If you hear nothing, push both pieces deeper into juicy flesh and check that they do not touch each other.
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Battery test a lemon holds one copper wire and one zinc nail.

flow.do: Make the same cell in a second lemon half. Twist the copper wire of the first half round the nail of the second. Test from the first nail to the second copper wire. Then untwist it, twist the two copper wires together, and test from nail to nail.
flow.say: Now two cells are joined in a row, copper to zinc. Will the crackle be louder, quieter or the same? Listen. Now I join copper to copper, so that the two cells face each other. What do you expect?
flow.kid: Join two lemon cells in a row. Is the crackle louder? Then join copper to copper. Listen again.

ask.q: Why did the crackle vanish when the two cells faced each other?
good: Each cell pushed the electrons the opposite way.
The two pushes cancelled out.

flow.parent: In a row, the two pushes add and the crackle is clearly louder. Facing each other, the pushes cancel and there is silence or a very faint tick.
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Battery test you join two lemon cells in a row, then turn one round.

flow.do: Make all four halves into cells and join them in a row, copper to zinc each time. Test from the free nail to the free copper wire. If you have a red LED, darken the room. Touch the LED's long leg to the free copper wire and its short leg to the free nail.
flow.say: Four cells in a row. Listen first. Now the room is dark. The long leg of the LED goes to the copper end and the short leg to the zinc end. Look closely at the LED.
flow.kid: Join four lemon cells in a row. Listen. In the dark, try the red LED.
flow.parent: With zinc nails, four cells give about 3.6 volts and a red LED glows faintly in a dark room. With foil strips the glow may need six cells, or may not show. The LED lights only one way round, so turn it if it stays dark.
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Battery test you join four lemon cells and try to light a red LED.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they heard, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below. Then twist the copper wire of one cell round its own nail and leave that lemon half until tomorrow.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you heard, and why you think it happened. Now we join this cell's copper to its own zinc, and leave it until tomorrow. Which piece of metal do you think will look different?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you heard. Say why.

ask.q: The lemon was the same in every test. So what makes the electrons flow?
good: The two metals being different.
One metal gives electrons and the other does not.

flow.parent: The reason: zinc gives away electrons more easily than copper. Zinc atoms leave their electrons in the nail and go into the juice. The electrons flow through the wire and the earphones to the copper. Two pieces of the same metal push equally, so nothing flows. The energy comes from the zinc, and the lemon is the path.
flow.think: If the zinc is giving something away all night, what should the nail look like tomorrow?
flow.context: In this step of the Lemon Battery test you say what the crackles show. You leave one lemon cell joined overnight.

flow.do: The next day, pull the zinc nail and the copper wire out of the lemon half that was left joined. Wipe both. Compare the part of each that was in the juice with the part that stayed dry. Then throw all the lemon halves away.
flow.say: Look at the part of the nail that sat in the juice, and the part that stayed dry. Now look at the copper wire in the same way. Which metal changed?
flow.kid: Pull out the nail and the wire. Which one looks different now?
flow.wait: Leave the joined lemon cell until the next day

check.q: After a night in a joined lemon cell, the zinc nail is dull and rough and the copper is unchanged. Why?
options: Zinc atoms gave away electrons and left the nail
The copper sucked the colour out of the zinc
Lemon juice makes all metals dull
check.why: Each zinc atom that gives away electrons becomes an ion and floats off into the juice. So the zinc is slowly used up. The copper only passes electrons on, so it stays as it was. If you chose 'all metals', look again at the copper.

flow.parent: The part of the nail that sat in the juice is dull, dark and rough, and the copper is bright. A foil strip is thin and pitted, and may have holes. Some zinc also dissolves straight into the acid without sending electrons round the wire.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Lemon Battery test. After one night you compare the zinc nail and the copper wire from a joined lemon cell.

experiments.title: Rust in Ten Minutes: which nail do the cells rust?
experiments.question: Two steel nails stand in salt water, joined to the two ends of a pack of four AA cells. A third nail stands in salt water alone. Which nail changes most in a few minutes, and what does it turn into?
experiments.predict: Before you join the wires, guess. Which nail will change most: the plus nail, the minus nail, or the nail standing alone? What will you see, and why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use three nails of the same kind and size. Put the same amount of water and salt in both glasses. Put each nail 3 centimetres deep. Keep both glasses side by side for the same time. The only thing that changes is what each nail is joined to.

materials.item: plain steel nails, not galvanised, about 5 to 7 centimetres long. Hardware shops call them bright wire nails
AA cells in a holder for four cells, which gives 6 volts. With no holder, a grown-up tapes four cells tightly end to end in a paper tube
pieces of thin plastic-covered wire, each 30 centimetres long, with 2 centimetres stripped bare at each end
clear glasses, each with 200 millilitres of tap water
salt, half a teaspoon for each glass
a strip of thick card longer than the glass is wide, with two holes 3 centimetres apart
a sheet of white paper to stand behind the glasses, sticky tape, tissue paper, a timer and a notebook page

experiments.safety: A grown-up builds the cell pack and joins the wires. Never let the two bare wire ends touch each other, because the cells get hot. Work near an open window and away from the stove. Do not taste the water. Never try this with a wall socket, a charger or an adapter.
experiments.record: Draw a table with rows for 1, 3 and 5 minutes. In each row, write what you see at the plus nail, the minus nail and the nail alone.
experiments.context: In this experiment four AA cells are joined to two steel nails in salt water. You watch which nail turns to rust within minutes.

setup.art: Two clear glasses of water side by side in front of a sheet of white paper, with a spoon of salt above each.
setup.caption: 1. Stir half a teaspoon of salt into each glass of water.

setup.art: A strip of card lying across the top of one glass with two steel nails pushed through it, their points in the water, and a third nail leaning alone in the second glass.
setup.caption: 2. Hang two nails in one glass, 3 centimetres apart. Stand one nail in the other glass.

setup.art: A holder with four AA cells, a red wire from its plus end twisted round the head of one nail and a black wire from its minus end twisted round the other.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up joins the plus wire to one nail and the minus wire to the other.

setup.art: The same glass a few minutes later: a stream of tiny bubbles rising from one nail and a greenish-brown cloud sinking from the other.
setup.caption: 4. Watch for five minutes. Write what each nail does.

setup.art: Three nails lying on a tissue: one dark and rough with brown smears, two still shiny.
setup.caption: 5. Take the wires off. Lay the three nails side by side.

flow.do: Show your child the three nails, the two glasses and the cell pack. Explain which nail will go where. Ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: These three nails are the same. Two will stand in salt water, joined to the plus and minus ends of four cells. One will stand in salt water alone. Which nail will change most in five minutes? What will you see, and why do you think so?
flow.kid: Three nails go into salt water. Two are joined to cells. Which will change most? Why?

ask.q: Why did you choose that nail?
good: The plus end pulls electrons out, so that nail might be eaten.
The minus end has more electrons, so something will happen there.
The nail alone is in salt water, and salt makes rust.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of Rust in Ten Minutes. You guess which of three nails in salt water will change most.

flow.do: Stir half a teaspoon of salt into each glass. Push two nails through the holes in the card and rest the card on one glass. The nails should reach 3 centimetres into the water and not touch. Lean the third nail in the other glass. Put the cells in the holder. Twist one wire round the head of each hanging nail, above the water.
flow.say: I am setting up the nails. The wires must stay above the water, so that only the nails are in it. I will not join the wires to the cells until you are ready to watch.
flow.kid: Stir in the salt. A grown-up hangs the nails and fixes the wires.
flow.parent: Write a plus sign and a minus sign on the card beside the two nails. Stand the white paper behind the glasses so the colours show.
flow.context: In this step of Rust in Ten Minutes a grown-up hangs two nails in salt water and prepares the cells.

flow.do: Join the two wires to the plus and minus ends of the cell pack. Start the timer. Watch both glasses for five minutes. At 1, 3 and 5 minutes your child says what each nail is doing, and you write it down.
flow.say: The wires are joined. Watch the plus nail, the minus nail and the nail alone. Tell me everything you see at each one.
flow.kid: Watch all three nails for five minutes. Say what each one does.
flow.parent: Fine bubbles stream from the minus nail at once. The plus nail makes few bubbles. Within a minute or two a green-grey cloud sinks from it, and the water slowly turns yellow, then brown. The nail alone shows nothing.
flow.context: In this step of Rust in Ten Minutes the cells are joined. You watch three nails in salt water for five minutes.

flow.do: Take the wires off the cell pack. Lift out all three nails and lay them side by side on tissue paper. Let your child wipe each one and compare them.
flow.say: The cells are off. Wipe each nail with tissue. Which nail has changed, and which two look as they did before?
flow.kid: Wipe the three nails. Which one changed? Which two stayed shiny?

check.q: In Rust in Ten Minutes, which nail turned dark and made a brown cloud?
options: The nail on the plus wire
The nail on the minus wire
The nail standing alone
check.why: The cells pull electrons out of the nail on the plus wire. Iron atoms that lose electrons leave the nail and become rust. The cells push electrons into the minus nail, so that nail loses none and stays clean. The nail alone would rust too, but over days.

flow.parent: The plus nail is dark, rough and smeared with brown. The minus nail is as shiny as before, or shinier.
flow.context: In this step of Rust in Ten Minutes you compare the three nails after five minutes in salt water.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below. Leave the cloudy glass for 15 minutes and look at the colour again. Then pour it down the sink and wash the glass with soap.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. What were the bubbles at the minus nail? Look at the cloudy water again in a quarter of an hour.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why.

ask.q: The nail alone sat in the same salt water. Why did that nail not rust in five minutes?
good: Nothing was pulling electrons out of it quickly.
The air does it slowly, over days.

ask.q: How could you use this to stop a steel pipe rusting?
good: Join the pipe to the minus end, so electrons are pushed into it.

flow.parent: The reason: the cells pull electrons out of the plus nail. Each iron atom that loses electrons becomes an ion and leaves the nail. In the water the iron ions join with oxygen and form rust, which turns orange-brown as it stands. The cells push electrons into the minus nail. Water molecules take them and split, and the bubbles are hydrogen gas. Rusting in air is the same loss of electrons, with oxygen pulling them slowly.
flow.think: Buried gas pipelines are joined to the minus end of a power supply. Why?
flow.context: This is the last step of Rust in Ten Minutes. You say why only the nail on the plus wire turned to rust.

experiments.title: Give It Back: can split water make earphones crackle?
experiments.question: Four AA cells split water into two gases on two pencil leads. When the cells are taken away, can the pencil leads and their gases push electrons back through earphones?
experiments.predict: Before the cells are joined, guess. After the cells are taken away, will the two pencils make the earphones crackle? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same two pencils, the same glass of baking soda water and the same earphones all through. Test the pencils with the earphones before the cells are joined, and again straight after. The only thing that changes is whether a current has just passed.

materials.item: wooden pencils, sharpened at both ends. Pull off any rubber first
a clear glass with 200 millilitres of tap water
baking soda (cooking soda), one level teaspoon
a strip of thick card longer than the glass is wide, with two holes 3 centimetres apart
AA cells in a holder for four cells, with a wire 30 centimetres long on each end
pieces of bare copper wire, each 10 centimetres long
wired earphones with a round plug
a torch or phone light, sticky tape, a timer and a notebook page

experiments.safety: A grown-up sharpens the pencils and joins the cells. Never let the two wires from the cells touch each other. Work away from the stove, because one of the gases is hydrogen.
experiments.record: Draw a table with three rows. The rows are before the cells, straight after 3 minutes of current, and after 1 more minute. Write the crackle and how long it lasted.
experiments.context: In this experiment four AA cells split water into hydrogen and oxygen on two pencil leads. Then you test whether the gases can give a current back.

setup.art: Two pencils sharpened at both ends pushed through a strip of card that rests on a glass of water, their lower tips in the water.
setup.caption: 1. Hang two pencils in baking soda water, 3 centimetres apart.

setup.art: A bare copper wire wound tightly round the top lead of each pencil and held with a small piece of tape.
setup.caption: 2. Wind a bare copper wire round the top lead of each pencil.

setup.art: A child with earphones in her ears pressing one copper wire on the earphone plug and scraping the tip on the other wire.
setup.caption: 3. Test the two wires with the earphones before any current has passed.

setup.art: A holder of four cells joined to the two copper wires, with fine bubbles rising from both pencil tips in the water and more bubbles at one of them.
setup.caption: 4. A grown-up joins the cells for 3 minutes. Watch the bubbles.

setup.art: The cell holder moved away to the side, and the child testing the two pencil wires with the earphone plug again.
setup.caption: 5. Take the cells away. Test with the earphones at once.

flow.do: Stir one level teaspoon of baking soda into the glass of water. Push the two pencils through the card and rest it on the glass. The lower leads must be in the water and not touching. Wind a bare copper wire tightly round the top lead of each pencil and tape it.
flow.say: Pencil lead is graphite, a kind of carbon that carries electricity. The baking soda gives the water ions, so that it can carry a current too. Both pencils are the same.
flow.kid: Stir in the soda. Hang two pencils in the water. Wind wire on each top.
flow.parent: The wire must touch the black lead, not the wood. Scrape a little wood away from the top lead if you need to.
flow.context: This is the first step of Give It Back. You hang two pencils in baking soda water and fix a wire to each.

flow.do: Put the earbuds in your child's ears. Press one copper wire on the band next to the plug's tip and scrape the tip on the other wire. Record the result. Then ask for the guess and the reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Listen first, before any cells are joined. What do you hear? Next, the cells will pass a current for three minutes, and then I will take them away. Will the pencils make a crackle then? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Test the two pencils with the earphones. Will they crackle after the cells? Why?

ask.q: Two pencils of the same graphite gave no crackle. Which earlier result does that match?
good: Two copper wires in a lemon gave no crackle in the Lemon Battery test.
Two electrodes that are the same give no push.

flow.parent: Expect silence now. The two leads are the same material in the same liquid, so neither pushes electrons to the other.
flow.context: In this step of Give It Back you test two pencils in baking soda water before any current has passed.

flow.do: Join one wire from the cell pack to each copper wire. Mark which pencil is on the minus wire. Shine the torch through the glass. Watch for 3 minutes. Ask your child which pencil makes more bubbles.
flow.say: The cells are joined. Look at the two pencil tips in the water. Where are the bubbles coming from? Which tip makes more?
flow.kid: Watch the pencil tips for three minutes. Which tip makes more bubbles?
flow.parent: Fine bubbles rise from both tips. The tip on the minus wire makes about twice as many. That gas is hydrogen, and the gas at the plus tip is oxygen. With only two cells the bubbles are few and slow.
flow.context: In this step of Give It Back four AA cells pass a current through baking soda water. Gas bubbles off two pencil tips.

flow.do: Take both cell wires off and move the cell pack right away. Within five seconds, test the two copper wires with the earphone plug as before. Keep scraping, and count the seconds until the crackle fades. Record the result.
flow.say: The cells are gone. Only the pencils and the water are left. Scrape the plug now, and keep scraping. What do you hear? Tell me when it fades.
flow.kid: The cells are gone. Scrape the plug at once. Count until the crackle fades.

check.q: In Give It Back, the cells were taken away and the pencils still made a crackle. What pushed the electrons?
options: The two gases on the leads, joining again
Electricity left over in the water
The earphones' own battery
check.why: After the current, one lead is coated with hydrogen and the other with oxygen. So the two electrodes are no longer the same. Hydrogen gives electrons, and they flow through the earphones to the oxygen side. If you chose 'left over in the water', remember that water does not store a current.

flow.parent: Expect a clear crackle that fades within about half a minute. Test quickly, because the gas on the leads is soon used up.
flow.context: In this step of Give It Back the cells are taken away. You test at once whether the two pencils make earphones crackle.

flow.do: When the crackle has gone, wait one minute and test again. Then join the cells for one more minute, take them away and test once more. Record both results.
flow.say: The crackle has faded. Does it come back if we simply wait? Now the cells go on for one more minute. Test again.
flow.kid: Wait one minute and test. Then join the cells again and test.
flow.parent: Waiting brings nothing back. One more minute of current brings the crackle back. So the crackle depends on the gases that the current makes.
flow.context: In this step of Give It Back you check when the crackle returns: after waiting, or after more current.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they heard, and why they think it happened. After they have answered, read them the explanation in the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you heard, and why you think it happened. Where did the energy for the crackle come from in the first place?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you heard. Say why.

ask.q: Where did the energy for the crackle come from?
good: From the AA cells, which split the water.
The cells put energy into the gases, and the gases gave it back.

flow.parent: The reason: the current split water into hydrogen at the minus lead and oxygen at the plus lead. That took energy from the cells. With the cells gone, hydrogen gives its electrons back through the earphones to the oxygen side, and water forms again. This is a small fuel cell. Some of the crackle also comes from charge held on the wet surface of the leads.
flow.think: A phone battery is charged, then used, then charged again. How is that like this experiment?
flow.context: This is the last step of Give It Back. You say why two pencils in water could make earphones crackle after the cells were removed.

activities.title: Battery Hunt: read the volts

materials.item: things at home that run on cells: a TV remote, a wall clock, a torch, a toy, a weighing scale
a notebook page and a pencil

activities.safety: A grown-up opens the cell covers. Button cells are dangerous if a small child swallows one, so put each one straight back.

schedule.what: Find five cells at home and read the volts printed on each.

activities.record: A table with three columns: the thing, the kind of cell, and the volts printed on the cell.
activities.context: In this activity you find five cells at home and read the number of volts printed on each one.

setup.art: A TV remote with its back cover off showing two AAA cells, next to a wall clock turned over to show one AA cell.
setup.caption: 1. Open five things at home that run on cells.

setup.art: A close view of an AA cell showing the print 1.5 V and the plus and minus signs at its ends.
setup.caption: 2. Find the volts and the plus and minus signs on each cell.

setup.art: A notebook table listing remote, clock, torch, toy and scale with a volts number beside each.
setup.caption: 3. Write the volts in a table and look for a pattern.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many cells are working in your home right now. Draw the table with three columns.
flow.say: How many cells do you think are working in our home at this moment? Count the ones in clocks, remotes, toys and torches. We will look at five of them.
flow.kid: Guess how many cells your home has. Draw a table with three columns.
flow.context: This is the first step of Battery Hunt. You guess how many cells are at work in your home.

flow.do: Open five things that run on cells. On each cell, find the plus sign, the minus sign and the number of volts. Your child writes them in the table. Put every cell back the right way round.
flow.say: Find the plus end and the minus end. Now find a number with the letter V after it. That is the number of volts.
flow.kid: Find the plus sign, the minus sign and the volts. Write them down.
flow.parent: AA and AAA cells say 1.5 V. Most button cells say 3 V or 1.5 V. A phone or power bank says about 3.7 V on its label. You do not need to open a phone.
flow.context: In this step of Battery Hunt you read the volts and the plus and minus signs on five cells.

flow.do: Look at the table together and talk about the questions below.
flow.say: Every cell has exactly two ends, a plus and a minus. A fat cell and a thin cell can both say 1.5 volts. What might the size change, if it does not change the volts?
flow.kid: A fat cell and a thin cell both say 1.5 volts. What is different?

ask.q: Why might every cell have exactly two ends?
good: Electrons leave from one end and come back at the other.
Something gives electrons and something else takes them.

ask.q: What does a bigger cell have more of?
good: More of the substances inside, so it lasts longer.

flow.parent: Volts depend on which substances are inside the cell. Size decides how long the cell lasts. Your child does not need the answer yet, because the Lemon Battery test gives it.
flow.context: This is the last step of Battery Hunt. You ask why every cell has two ends and why size does not change the volts.

activities.title: Not Only Lemons: what can sit between the two metals?

materials.item: a zinc nail (a galvanised nail) and a 10 centimetre piece of bare copper wire
wired earphones with a round plug
small bowls or katoris
half a cup of water with half a teaspoon of salt stirred in
half a cup of tamarind water or vinegar
half a cup of plain tap water
two tablespoons of cooking oil
a raw potato cut in half
a dry cloth, soap, and a notebook page

schedule.what: Test a zinc nail and a copper wire in five things from the kitchen.

activities.record: A table with five rows: salt water, tamarind water, potato, tap water and oil. Beside each, write 'none', 'faint' or 'loud'.
activities.context: In the Lemon Battery test, a zinc nail and a copper wire in a lemon made earphones crackle. In this activity you test the same two metals in five other things.

setup.art: Four small steel bowls in a row holding salt water, brown tamarind water, plain water and yellow oil, with half a potato beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Set out salt water, tamarind water, tap water, oil and half a potato.

setup.art: A hand holding a grey nail and a copper wire 2 centimetres apart in a bowl of liquid.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the zinc nail and the copper wire in each one, 2 centimetres apart.

setup.art: A child with earphones scraping the earphone plug on the head of the nail while the copper wire is pressed on the plug's band.
setup.caption: 3. Listen for a crackle. Write none, faint or loud.

flow.do: Set out the four bowls and the potato. Ask your child to guess which ones will give a crackle, and why. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: In the Lemon Battery test, zinc and copper in a lemon made a crackle. Was the lemon special? Here are salt water, tamarind water, a potato, tap water and oil. Which will work, and why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which will crackle: salt water, tamarind, potato, tap water or oil? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of Not Only Lemons. You guess which kitchen things can take the lemon's place in a cell.

flow.do: Test the salt water first. Hold the nail and the wire in it, 2 centimetres apart and not touching. Press the wire on the band next to the plug's tip and scrape the tip on the nail. Record the result. Wipe both metals dry. Test the tamarind water, the potato and the tap water the same way. Test the oil last.
flow.say: Hold the two metals in the bowl without letting them touch. Scrape the plug on the nail. Is the crackle loud, faint or missing? Wipe both metals before the next bowl.
flow.kid: Hold both metals in each bowl. Scrape the plug. Loud, faint or none?
flow.parent: Salt water and tamarind water give a loud crackle. The potato gives a clear one. Tap water gives a faint one. Oil gives none. Wash the oil off the metals with soap afterwards.
flow.context: In this step of Not Only Lemons you listen to zinc and copper in five kitchen things.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child what the loud ones share. Then read them the note below.
flow.say: Which ones worked, and which did not? What do the ones that worked have in common? What does oil lack?
flow.kid: Which ones worked? What do they share? What is missing from oil?

check.q: A zinc nail and a copper wire crackle in salt water but not in cooking oil. Why?
options: Salt water has ions and oil has none
Oil is too thick to hear through
Salt water is colder than oil
check.why: A cell needs a liquid with ions in it, called an electrolyte. The ions carry charge between the two metals inside the liquid. Salt, acids and the juices of plants all give ions. Oil has none, so the loop is never complete.

flow.parent: The lemon is not special. Any liquid with ions in it works. Tap water has a few ions from dissolved minerals, so it works a little.
flow.context: This is the last step of Not Only Lemons. You work out what a liquid needs so that two metals in it make a cell.

activities.title: Electric Writing: which wire writes red on turmeric paper?

materials.item: turmeric powder, half a teaspoon, and salt, a quarter teaspoon
three tablespoons of water in a small bowl, and a ball of cotton
half a page of plain white paper
a piece of kitchen foil about 15 centimetres square, on a steel plate
a wooden pencil sharpened at both ends
AA cells in a holder for four cells, with a wire 30 centimetres long on each end
sticky tape

activities.safety: A grown-up joins the cells. Never let the two wires from the cells touch each other. Turmeric stains cloth, so cover the table.

schedule.what: Make damp turmeric paper and write on it with a pencil joined to four cells.

activities.record: Keep the paper. Beside each mark, write which end of the cells the pencil was joined to.
activities.context: In this activity a pencil joined to four AA cells writes on damp turmeric paper. You find out which end of the cells makes a red mark.

setup.art: A child wiping yellow turmeric water over half a sheet of white paper with a ball of cotton.
setup.caption: 1. Wipe turmeric and salt water over the paper until it is yellow and damp.

setup.art: The damp yellow paper lying on a square of kitchen foil on a steel plate, with a wire taped to the corner of the foil.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the paper on foil. Tape the plus wire to the foil.

setup.art: A pencil with a wire wound round its top lead writing on the yellow paper and leaving a red-brown line.
setup.caption: 3. Join the minus wire to the pencil's top lead. Write slowly.

setup.art: The paper turned over to show red-brown patches on its underside.
setup.caption: 4. Swap the two wires. Write again, then look under the paper.

flow.do: Stir the turmeric and the salt into the three tablespoons of water. Your child wipes it over the paper with the cotton until the paper is yellow and damp all over. It should not drip.
flow.say: Turmeric is yellow in water and turns red in a base, such as soap. We will use the paper to show where a base forms.
flow.kid: Wipe turmeric water over the paper. Make it yellow and damp.
flow.context: This is the first step of Electric Writing. You make a sheet of damp yellow turmeric paper.

flow.do: Lay the foil on the plate and the damp paper on the foil. Tape the bare end of the plus wire to a corner of the foil. Wind the bare end of the minus wire round the pencil's top lead and tape it. Ask for the guess and the reason.
flow.say: The foil is joined to the plus end of the cells. The pencil is joined to the minus end. When the pencil touches the paper, will it leave a mark? What colour, and why do you think so?
flow.kid: The pencil is joined to the minus end. Will it leave a mark? Why?
flow.parent: The wire must touch the pencil's black lead. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: In this step of Electric Writing a grown-up joins the foil and the pencil to four AA cells. You guess what will happen.

flow.do: Your child holds the pencil by the wood and writes slowly on the damp paper, pressing lightly. They write their name or draw a shape.
flow.say: Write slowly, about one centimetre each second. What colour is the line? Lift the pencil. Does the line stay?
flow.kid: Write slowly on the damp paper. What colour is the line?
flow.parent: A red-brown line appears under the pencil tip and stays. If nothing shows, the paper is too dry or a wire has come loose.
flow.context: In this step of Electric Writing you write on damp turmeric paper. The pencil is joined to the minus end of four cells.

flow.do: Swap the two wires on the cell pack. Now the pencil is on the plus end and the foil is on the minus end. Your child writes on a fresh part of the paper for one minute. Then lift the paper and look at the underside.
flow.say: Now the pencil is on the plus end. Write again. Is there a red line? Now turn the paper over. What do you see where it lay on the foil?
flow.kid: Swap the wires. Write again. Then look under the paper.
flow.parent: The pencil now leaves no red line. Red-brown patches show on the underside, where the damp paper touched the foil. The red always forms at the minus side.
flow.context: In this step of Electric Writing the wires are swapped. You look for red marks on both sides of the turmeric paper.

flow.do: Talk about the question below. Then read your child the note.
flow.say: The red formed at the pencil when the pencil was minus. It formed at the foil when the foil was minus. What happens to water at the minus side?
flow.kid: The red always formed at the minus side. Why?

check.q: In Electric Writing, turmeric paper turns red where the minus wire touches. What forms there?
options: A base, left when water is split
An acid, from the lemon
Rust, from the pencil
check.why: The cells push electrons in at the minus side. Water molecules take them and split. Hydrogen gas leaves, and what stays behind is a base. Turmeric turns red in a base. A pencil lead is carbon and holds no iron, so it is not rust.

flow.parent: This is the electrolysis of water at one electrode. It is also why a swallowed button cell is so dangerous. The same base forms on the wet wall of the food pipe.
flow.context: This is the last step of Electric Writing. You work out why turmeric paper turns red at the minus side.

activities.title: Electron Path: move the coins round a lemon cell

materials.item: a large sheet of paper, or two notebook pages taped together, and a pencil
small coins or rajma beans, to stand for electrons
buttons or pieces of chana, to stand for metal ions

schedule.what: Draw a lemon cell and a rusting drop, and move coins to show where the electrons go.

activities.record: Keep both drawings. On each, draw arrows to show the path the coins took.
activities.context: In the Lemon Battery test a zinc nail and a copper wire in a lemon made earphones crackle. In this activity you move coins on a drawing to show where the electrons went.

setup.art: A large pencil drawing of a lemon with a nail and a wire in it, joined by a loop that passes through a small drawing of earphones.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a big lemon cell: nail, copper wire, and a loop through the earphones.

setup.art: Six small coins placed on the drawn nail and three buttons beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Put six coins on the nail as electrons, and three buttons as zinc atoms.

setup.art: A child's hand sliding two coins along the drawn loop towards the copper wire while one button sits in the drawn juice.
setup.caption: 3. Move one button into the juice. Slide two coins round the loop to the copper.

flow.do: Your child draws a lemon as large as the page. Inside it they draw a zinc nail on the left and a copper wire on the right. They join the two tops with a loop that passes through a small pair of earphones. Put six coins and three buttons on the nail.
flow.say: Draw the lemon cell from the Lemon Battery test. The coins are electrons. Each button is a zinc atom in the nail. Each zinc atom has two electrons that it holds loosely.
flow.kid: Draw a big lemon cell. Put six coins and three buttons on the nail.
flow.context: This is the first step of Electron Path. You draw a lemon cell and lay out coins as electrons.

flow.do: Your child moves one button off the nail into the juice. For that button, they slide two coins up the nail and round the loop. The coins pass through the earphones and down the copper wire. They do this three times. Then ask the questions below.
flow.say: One zinc atom leaves the nail as an ion. The two electrons it leaves behind go round the wire to the copper. Do it for all three. What has the nail lost? What would happen if both sides were zinc?
flow.kid: Move one button into the juice. Slide two coins round the loop. Repeat.

ask.q: What has the nail lost by the end?
good: Three zinc atoms, which are now ions in the juice.
The nail is being used up.

ask.q: What if both pieces were zinc?
good: Both would push equally, so no coins would move.

flow.parent: At the copper, the electrons are taken by hydrogen ions in the juice. Your child can draw small circles marked H there.
flow.context: In this step of Electron Path you move coins round a drawn lemon cell to show electrons leaving the zinc.

flow.do: On the back of the page, your child draws a thick steel plate seen from the side. They draw a drop of water on top. They put a button under the middle of the drop and two coins beside it. They move the button up into the drop. They slide the coins through the plate to the edge of the drop.
flow.say: This is a drop of water on steel. An iron atom under the middle leaves as an ion. Its two electrons travel through the steel to the edge of the drop. Oxygen takes them there. Where is the wire this time?
flow.kid: Draw a drop on steel. Move the button up. Slide the coins sideways.

check.q: When a drop of water rusts a steel plate, what do the electrons travel through?
options: The steel plate itself
The air above the drop
A copper wire
check.why: Steel is a metal, so electrons move through it easily. The plate does the job of the wire. The electrons leave the iron under the middle of the drop and reach the oxygen at the edge.

flow.parent: This is why rusting counts as a cell with no outside wire. The energy becomes a tiny amount of heat.
flow.context: This is the last step of Electron Path. You move coins on a drawing of a water drop on steel to show how rust starts.

projects.title: The Bodyguard Nail: can another metal save a nail from rust?

materials.item: plain steel nails, not galvanised, about 5 centimetres long
a zinc nail (a galvanised nail). If you have none, use a strip of kitchen foil 10 centimetres by 3
a piece of bare copper wire 15 centimetres long
clear glasses or jars of the same size
salt, half a teaspoon for each glass, and water
a small rubber band, a dry cloth, three paper labels and a notebook page

projects.safety: The nails are sharp. A grown-up strips the copper wire. Do not drink the water, and wash your hands after touching the nails.

schedule.what: Set up three nails in salt water: one alone, one with zinc, one with copper. Write your guess.
Look at each nail and give its rust a score from 0 to 4.
Score once more, take the nails out and say what you found.

projects.record: A table with three rows, for the nail alone, the nail with zinc and the nail with copper. Each day write a rust score from 0 to 4. A score of 0 means no rust, and 4 means the nail is covered.
projects.context: In this four-day project three steel nails sit in salt water. One is alone, one touches zinc and one is wrapped in copper. You find out whether a second metal changes how fast a nail rusts.

setup.art: Three steel nails on a table: one alone, one held against a grey galvanised nail by a rubber band, and one with copper wire wound tightly round it.
setup.caption: 1. Leave one nail alone. Band one to a zinc nail. Wind copper wire round one.

setup.art: Three labelled glasses in a row, each with a little salt water and one of the nails lying on the bottom.
setup.caption: 2. Lay each nail in its own glass of salt water, 3 centimetres deep.

setup.art: A notebook table with three rows and four columns of rust scores, and the three glasses behind it, two of them with orange water.
setup.caption: 3. Each day, give each nail a rust score from 0 to 4.

flow.do: Day 1. Rub the three plain nails with the dry cloth. Leave nail A alone. Hold nail B tightly against the zinc nail with the rubber band. Wind the copper wire tightly round nail C, about ten turns. Stir half a teaspoon of salt into water in each glass, 3 centimetres deep. Lay one nail in each glass and label them. Ask for the guess and the reason.
flow.say: All three nails are the same steel, in the same salt water. Nail A is alone. Nail B touches zinc. Nail C is wrapped in copper. After three days, which nail will have the most rust and which the least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One nail is alone. One touches zinc. One has copper. Which will rust most? Why?
flow.parent: The metals must touch each other firmly, metal to metal. Keep the three glasses together, away from direct sun. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Bodyguard Nail. You set up three nails in salt water and guess which will rust most.

flow.do: Day 2. Look at each glass without moving the nails. Your child gives each plain nail a rust score from 0 to 4 and writes down anything else they see.
flow.say: Look at nail A, nail B and nail C. Score the rust on each plain nail from 0 to 4. What else has changed in each glass?
flow.kid: Score the rust on each nail from 0 to 4. What else changed?
flow.wait: Do this the day after you set up the nails
flow.parent: Nail A usually shows orange specks by now. Nail B is usually still grey, with white fluff near the zinc. Nail C usually has as much rust as A, or more.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Bodyguard Nail. You score the rust on three nails that have spent one day in salt water.

flow.do: Day 3. Look and score again in the same way.
flow.say: Score each nail again. Which score has gone up most since yesterday? Is any nail still at zero?
flow.kid: Score each nail again. Which score went up most?
flow.wait: Do this two days after you set up the nails
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Bodyguard Nail. You score the rust on the three nails again.

flow.do: Day 4. Score once more. Lift out the nails and lay them on paper. Take off the rubber band and unwind the copper. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. Then read them the note below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Look at the zinc nail too. What has happened to its coat?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why.
flow.wait: Do this three days after you set up the nails

check.q: A steel nail touching zinc in salt water stays grey, while a nail alone rusts. Why?
options: The zinc gives the electrons, so the iron keeps its own
The zinc soaks up all the salt
The rubber band keeps the water out
check.why: Zinc is above iron on the metal ladder, so zinc gives away electrons more easily. While zinc touches the nail, the zinc corrodes and the iron is spared. The white fluff is corroded zinc. Copper is below iron, so next to copper the iron is the one that gives electrons.

flow.parent: The zinc nail is dull and may be patchy, because its coat was eaten in place of the steel. With foil in place of zinc, the protection is weaker and the foil turns pitted. If nail A and nail C look the same, write that down. It is a real result.
flow.context: This is the last day of the Bodyguard Nail. You compare a nail alone, a nail with zinc and a nail with copper after three days in salt water.

challenges.title: The Kitchen Pile: build a battery with no lemon
challenges.problem: In 1800 Alessandro Volta built the first battery from a pile of metal discs and wet card. Build your own pile from kitchen things. It must give a louder crackle in earphones than one lemon cell does.
constraints: No lemon or other fruit, and no shop cells.
Use only kitchen foil, copper wire or coins, paper, salt, vinegar or tamarind water.
At most six cells in the pile.
The pile must stand by itself on a plate while you test it.
materials: four to six pieces of bare copper wire, each 10 centimetres long, each wound into a flat spiral
a few steel one-rupee or two-rupee coins, to try in place of copper
newspaper or tissue paper cut into squares 3 centimetres wide
a small bowl of water with a teaspoon of salt and a teaspoon of vinegar or tamarind water
wired earphones with a round plug
a red LED, if you have one
general: Make one cell as a sandwich. Lay down a square of foil, then a square of wet paper, then a copper spiral.
Stack the next cell straight on top, so that its foil sits on the copper below it.
Squeeze each paper square so that it is wet but does not drip down the side of the pile.
creative: Try steel coins in place of copper spirals, and compare the crackle.
Make the squares larger, so that more metal touches the wet paper.
Test whether warm salt water gives a louder crackle than cold.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own pile. Draw it and label each layer. Test it against one lemon cell, and write which crackle was louder. Then change one thing and test again.
challenges.context: In the Lemon Battery test a zinc nail and a copper wire in a lemon made earphones crackle. In this challenge you build a battery from foil, copper and wet paper, with no lemon.
