flow.do: Read the problem together. Lay out the materials. Ask your child what each layer of a cell must be.
flow.say: A cell needs two different metals and something with ions between them. Which things on this table can be the two metals? Which can carry the ions?
flow.kid: A cell needs two metals and a wet layer. Which things will you use?

ask.q: Why must the wet paper not touch the cell above or below?
good: The liquid would join two cells and spoil the pile.
Each cell must be separate, like the lemon halves on their own lids.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Kitchen Pile. You plan a battery made from foil, copper and wet paper.

flow.do: Your child builds one cell on the plate: foil, a wet paper square, a copper spiral. Test it with the earphones, with the band on the foil and the tip scraping the copper. Then build a lemon cell and test that for comparison.
flow.say: Build one sandwich and test it. Is there a crackle? How does it compare with one lemon cell?
flow.kid: Build one sandwich of foil, wet paper and copper. Test it.
flow.parent: One foil and copper cell gives a fainter crackle than a lemon cell with a zinc nail. That is expected, because foil has a thin skin that slows it.
flow.context: In this step of the Kitchen Pile you build one cell from foil, wet paper and copper, and test it.

flow.do: Your child stacks more cells on the first, up to six. Each foil must sit on the copper below it. Test from the bottom foil to the top copper after each new cell.
flow.say: Add one cell at a time, and test each time. Does every new cell make the crackle louder? If the crackle drops, look for wet paper that touches two cells.
flow.kid: Stack more cells. Test after each one. Does it get louder?
flow.parent: Three or four cells usually beat one lemon cell. If you have a red LED, try it in a dark room across five or six cells. It may glow very faintly, or not at all.
flow.context: In this step of the Kitchen Pile you stack cells and test whether each one adds to the crackle.

flow.do: Your child changes one thing, such as the size of the squares or the second metal, and tests again. Talk about the question below.
flow.say: Change one thing only, and test again. Did it help? How do you know it was that change?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Did it help?

ask.q: Why change only one thing at a time?
good: Then I know which change made the difference.

flow.parent: Praise a clear account of what was changed and what happened, more than a loud crackle.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Kitchen Pile. You change one thing in your pile and test it again.

items.p: What does a lemon cell need so that electrons flow through a wire?
opts: Two different metals in the juice
Two pieces of the same metal
A very sour lemon and nothing else
A lemon that has been warmed
items.why: One metal must give away electrons more easily than the other. Two pieces of the same metal push equally, so nothing flows.

items.p: A liquid with ions in it, such as lemon juice or salt water, is called an ____.
items.why: The ions in an electrolyte carry charge through the liquid. Without them the loop is not complete.

items.p: The electricity of a lemon battery comes out of the lemon.
items.why: False. The energy comes from the zinc as it gives away electrons and is used up. The lemon only gives the juice that carries the ions. Salt water works in its place.

items.p: Match each part of a lemon cell to its job.
pairs: The copper wire in the lemon
Passes electrons on to the juice
items.why: Each part has one job. Take any one away and the loop is broken, so the current stops.

items.p: In a lemon cell with zinc and copper, which metal is slowly used up?
items.why: Each zinc atom that gives away electrons becomes an ion and leaves the nail. The copper only passes electrons on.

items.p: Put these steps in order, to show how electrons travel in a lemon cell.
items: A zinc atom leaves two electrons in the nail
The electrons flow along the wire
Hydrogen ions in the juice take them
a: A zinc atom leaves two electrons in the nail
The electrons flow along the wire
Hydrogen ions in the juice take them
items.why: Electrons start at the metal that gives them and end at whatever takes them. The wire and the earphones are on the way.

items.p: Two lemon cells joined in a row push harder than one.
items.why: True. Cells joined copper to zinc add their pushes. Two cells of 0.9 volts give about 1.8 volts.

items.p: The unit that tells how hard a cell pushes electrons is the ____.
items.why: An AA cell pushes with 1.5 volts. A lemon cell pushes with about 0.9 volts.

items.p: Which two gases does an electric current split water into?
items.why: A water molecule is two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. A current separates them. Steam is still water.

items.p: Sort these. Must each one be present for iron to rust?
items.why: Rust forms when iron gives electrons to oxygen with water present. Salt only makes it faster.

items.p: Why does a cycle rust faster near the sea than far inland?
opts: Salty, damp air carries ions well
items.why: Salt water is a good electrolyte. It lets the tiny cells on the iron's surface work faster.

items.p: Two copper wires in a lemon give no crackle in earphones. Explain why.
items.a: Both wires are the same metal, so both hold their electrons equally strongly. Neither gives electrons to the other, so no electrons flow.
items.why: A strong answer says that a cell needs a difference between its two metals.

items.p: Name two ways to stop an iron gate rusting. Say how each one works.
items.a: Paint keeps water and air off the iron. A coat of zinc gives away electrons in place of the iron. So the zinc corrodes and the iron does not.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different ways and says what each does. One blocks water and oxygen, and the other gives electrons.

items.p: Draw a lemon cell. Label the zinc, the copper and the way the electrons flow.
items.a: A lemon with a zinc nail and a copper wire in it, joined outside by a wire. An arrow on the outside wire points from the zinc to the copper.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two different metals and a complete loop. The arrow must run from zinc to copper through the outside wire.
items.art: A blank box with the outline of half a lemon in the middle.

items.p: What is a galvanised bucket coated with?
items.why: Galvanised means coated with zinc. The zinc corrodes in place of the steel under it.

items.p: Which pair is furthest apart on the metal ladder, and so pushes hardest in a cell?
items.why: Magnesium is at the top of the ladder and gold is at the bottom. Copper and copper are on the same rung and give no push.

items.p: Four lemon cells give 3.6 volts, yet they cannot light a torch bulb. Why?
opts: Too few electrons pass each second
The bulb is the wrong colour
items.why: Volts say how hard the cells push. A torch bulb also needs many electrons each second, and a lemon passes very few.

items.p: When a current splits water, which gas comes off at the minus electrode?
items.why: The cells push electrons into the minus electrode. Water molecules take them and split, and hydrogen bubbles off.

items.p: Charging a phone pushes the change inside its battery backwards.
items.why: True. The charger's current forces the change the other way. That is electrolysis inside the battery.

items.p: Stainless steel can never rust.
items.why: False. Its thin skin of chromium oxide can break down in salty water or sea air. Then brown spots and pits form.

items.p: Three of these stop rust by keeping water and air off the iron. Which one works differently?
items.why: Paint, oil and plastic are barriers. A zinc block lets water reach the iron, and gives away electrons in the iron's place.

items.p: One lemon cell gives 0.9 volts. How many cells joined in a row give 4.5 volts?
items.why: Cells in a row add their volts. 0.9 added five times is 4.5.

items.p: Put these metals in order, from the easiest giver of electrons to the strongest holder.
items.why: This is their order on the metal ladder. It is why zinc protects iron, and why gold is found as metal.

items.p: Sort these. Does a chemical change make the current, or does a current force the change?
cats: A chemical change makes a current
A current forces a chemical change
items: A chemical change makes a current
an AA cell in a clock
A chemical change makes a current
a fuel cell in a bus
A chemical change makes a current
A current forces a chemical change
A current forces a chemical change
A current forces a chemical change
items.why: The first group are batteries, where a chemical change makes the current. The second group are electrolysis, where a current forces the change. Each one is the other run backwards.

items.p: Two nails in salt water are joined to cells. Only the nail on the plus wire rusts. Explain why.
items.a: The cells pull electrons out of the plus nail. Iron atoms that lose electrons become ions and leave the nail, and they form rust. The cells push electrons into the minus nail, so it loses none.
items.why: A strong answer says that rusting is iron losing electrons, and that only the plus nail is losing them.

items.p: A galvanised bucket gets a deep scratch. Explain why the bare steel in the scratch still does not rust.
items.a: The zinc around the scratch still touches the steel. Zinc gives away electrons more easily than iron, so the zinc corrodes and the iron keeps its electrons.
items.why: A strong answer says that zinc protects by giving electrons, and not only by covering the steel.

items.p: When water is split, twice as much hydrogen comes off as oxygen. Explain why.
items.a: Each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom. So splitting water sets free two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom.
items.why: A strong answer links the two-to-one amounts of gas to what a water molecule is made of.

items.p: A town wants to store its midday solar power for the evening. People suggest different ways.

views.who: An engineer who builds lithium-ion batteries
views.says: Batteries give back nine tenths of the energy put in. Nothing else wastes so little.

views.who: An engineer who builds hydrogen plants
views.says: Split water with the spare power. Hydrogen can be kept for months, and batteries cannot do that.

views.who: A farmer who lives near a lithium mine
views.says: The mine uses our water. Count that cost before you buy thousands of batteries.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that splitting water and joining it again loses more than half the energy. Another is that every battery's metals must be mined.
items.why: Each view is partly right. A strong answer uses what the unit says about batteries and electrolysis, and takes the other costs seriously.

items.p: Label three parts of this AA cell cut in half: the zinc can, the black paste and the carbon rod.
a: The zinc can: the outer metal wall, which gives away electrons
The black paste: it holds manganese dioxide, which takes the electrons
The carbon rod: the dark rod down the middle, which collects electrons
items.why: A shop cell has the same parts as a lemon cell. It has a giver of electrons, a taker, and a paste with ions between them.
items.art: A side view of an AA cell cut in half lengthwise, showing a thin outer metal wall, a black filling and a dark rod down the middle, with three blank label lines.

items.p: A steel bolt sits in an aluminium window frame near the sea. Which metal corrodes first?
items.why: Aluminium is above iron on the metal ladder. Where the two touch in salty damp air, the aluminium gives the electrons.

items.p: Someone says the lemon is the source of a lemon battery's electricity. Which test checks this best?
opts: Try the same metals in salt water
items.why: If the metals still give a current with no lemon at all, the lemon cannot be the source. The other tests all keep the lemon.

items.p: A pile of six foil and copper cells crackles less than a pile of three. What is the likeliest fault?
opts: Wet paper is joining two cells together
items.why: Each cell must be separate. If liquid runs down the side and joins two cells, those cells stop adding their pushes.

items.p: Engineers join a buried steel pipeline to one end of a power supply to stop rust. Which end?
opts: The minus end, which pushes electrons in
The plus end, which pulls electrons out
items.why: Iron rusts by losing electrons. A pipe joined to the minus end is given electrons, so it loses none. A nail on the plus wire rusts in minutes.

items.p: Iron is found in the ground only as ore, but gold is found as metal. Why?
opts: Gold holds its electrons far more strongly
items.why: Iron gives electrons to oxygen easily, so over time it all joins with oxygen. Gold is at the bottom of the metal ladder and stays as metal.

items.p: A cell with more volts always lasts longer.
items.why: False. Volts say how hard a cell pushes. How long it lasts depends on how much of its substances are left to use up.

items.p: When a steel plate rusts under a drop of water, the steel itself carries the electrons.
items.why: True. The electrons travel through the metal from the middle of the drop to its edge. The plate does the job of a wire.

items.p: Match each change to the thing that gives away the electrons.
pairs: A lemon cell with zinc and copper
A fuel cell in a bus
items.why: In every one of these, electrons leave one substance and go to another. The only thing that differs is which substance gives the electrons.

items.p: Split water gives 2 litres of hydrogen for each litre of oxygen. How much hydrogen comes with 7 litres of oxygen?
items.why: There is twice as much hydrogen as oxygen. 7 times 2 is 14.

items.p: The slow change of a metal as it gives electrons to oxygen is called ____.
items.why: Rust is the corrosion of iron. Copper, silver, zinc and aluminium corrode too, each in its own way.

items.p: Two pencils in water crackle in earphones just after a current has split the water. What stored the energy?
items.a: The hydrogen and oxygen on the pencil leads stored it. The current used energy to split water into the two gases. When the gases joined again, they gave some of that energy back.
items.why: A strong answer says the energy was stored in the separated gases, and not in the water as 'electricity'.

items.p: Plan a fair test: does warm salt water rust a nail faster than cold salt water?
items.a: Use two nails of the same kind and two glasses with the same amount of water and salt. Keep one glass warm and one cold. Look at both after the same time and compare the rust.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the warmth, and keeps the nails, the salt, the water and the time the same.

items.p: A boat owner paints the zinc blocks on a steel boat to make them last. Why is this a mistake?
items.a: The zinc protects the steel by corroding in its place. Under paint, the sea water does not reach the zinc, so it gives no electrons. Then the steel corrodes.
items.why: A strong answer says the zinc works by being eaten, so saving the zinc gives up the steel.

items.p: Write one way a torch cell and a rusting gate are the same, and one way they differ.
items.a: Same: in both, a metal gives away electrons to something else and is used up. Different: in the cell the electrons go through a wire and can light a bulb. In the gate they do no useful work.
items.why: A strong answer names the passing of electrons as what they share, and the wire as the difference.

items.p: A city must choose new buses to replace its diesel ones. People disagree about which kind.

views.says: Hydrogen buses give out only water. Their tanks fill in ten minutes, like diesel.
Making hydrogen from water loses over half the energy. Battery buses use the same solar power far better.
A battery bus must stop for hours to charge. I need a bus that runs all day.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say what you would measure to decide.
items.a: Any view with a reason. One reason is that splitting water uses more energy than the hydrogen gives back. A good measurement is how far each bus goes on the same amount of solar power.
items.why: Working engineers hold each of these views. A strong answer uses what electrolysis costs in energy, and suggests a fair comparison.

items.p: Draw a water drop on steel. Show where iron is eaten, where the electrons go and where rust forms.
items.a: A drop on a plate, with a pit under the middle of the drop. Arrows run through the metal from the middle to the edge. A ring of rust lies near the edge.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the eaten spot and the rust in different places, joined by electrons moving through the steel.
items.art: A blank box with a thick grey bar across the bottom and the outline of a drop sitting on it.

quiz.p: Which pair, pushed into a lemon, makes electrons flow through a wire?
opts: A zinc nail and a copper wire
quiz.why: The two metals must be different. Zinc gives away electrons more easily than copper, so electrons flow from zinc to copper.

quiz.p: Why do two pieces of the same metal in a lemon give no current?
opts: Neither gives electrons more easily than the other
The same metal is too clean
The lemon only works with copper
quiz.why: A current needs a difference. Two pieces of one metal sit on the same rung of the metal ladder, so there is no push.

quiz.p: Where does the energy of a lemon battery come from?
opts: The zinc, as it is used up
quiz.why: The zinc changes as it gives away electrons, and that change gives the energy. The lemon is the path, and salt water can replace it.

opts: How hard a cell pushes electrons
How many cells are in a pack
quiz.why: Volts tell the push. How long a cell lasts depends on how much of its substances are left.

quiz.p: Three lemon cells of 0.9 volts each are joined in a row. What do they give together?
quiz.why: Cells in a row add their pushes. 0.9 added three times is 2.7.

opts: Using a current to force a chemical change
Rubbing two things to make charge
Mixing an acid with a base
quiz.why: In electrolysis the current comes from outside and forces a change, such as splitting water. It is a battery's change run backwards.

quiz.p: A current splits water. How do the amounts of the two gases compare?
opts: Twice as much hydrogen as oxygen
Twice as much oxygen as hydrogen
quiz.why: A water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, so twice as much hydrogen is set free.

quiz.p: Which three things together make iron rust?
quiz.why: Iron gives electrons to oxygen, and water must be there for it to happen. Salt only speeds it up.

quiz.p: Why does salt water rust iron faster than plain water?
quiz.why: Rusting works like a tiny cell on the iron's surface. Salt water is a good electrolyte, so the cell works faster.

quiz.p: How does a coat of zinc protect steel?
opts: Zinc gives electrons in place of the iron
quiz.why: Zinc is above iron on the metal ladder. While the two touch, the zinc corrodes and the iron is spared, even at a scratch.

quiz.p: A test changes the metals, the liquid and the earphones all at once. What is wrong with it?
opts: You cannot tell which change mattered
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing and keeps the rest the same. Then any difference in the result comes from that one thing.

quiz.p: How is a rusting gate like a battery?
opts: In both, a metal gives away electrons
Both store charge to use later
quiz.why: Rusting and a battery are the same kind of change. In the battery the electrons pass through a wire on the way.

applications: Steel boats and ships carry blocks of zinc on the hull. The zinc corrodes, and the steel is spared.
Roofing sheets, buckets, lamp posts and fence wire are galvanised. Their coat of zinc keeps them free of rust for decades.
Buried pipelines for gas, oil and water are joined to the minus end of a power supply. The current keeps them from losing electrons.
Aluminium is made from its ore by electrolysis, using huge currents. Recycling a can saves most of that electricity.
Gold-plated jewellery and shiny chrome taps get their thin coat of metal by electrolysis.
Phones, electric scooters, e-rickshaws and electric buses all run on cells that are charged by pushing their change backwards.
Spacecraft have used fuel cells, which join hydrogen and oxygen to give current and drinking water.

open_questions.q: Can a good battery be made from common things such as sodium, iron and sulfur?
open_questions.why_open: Lithium and cobalt are scarce, and mining them harms land and people. Batteries made from common elements exist, but so far they hold less energy or wear out sooner.

open_questions.q: Can water be split cheaply without rare metals?
open_questions.why_open: The best electrolysers use platinum and iridium, which are among the rarest metals on Earth. Many teams are testing cheaper materials, and none yet lasts as long.

open_questions.q: How did the dust of Mars turn to iron oxide?
open_questions.why_open: Some scientists think the iron rusted in water long ago. Others think it happened slowly in dry air. A study in 2025 found a mineral that forms in cold water, but the question is not closed.

open_questions.q: Did life begin at a natural electrical difference on the sea floor?
open_questions.why_open: Every living cell runs on a difference of ions across its wall. Deep-sea vents offer such a difference ready-made. Nobody has yet made life start in a laboratory copy of a vent.

open_questions.q: Where exactly does the first pit of rust start on a smooth piece of metal?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can now watch metal surfaces almost atom by atom. They still cannot say in advance which spot will give way first.

maths.problem: A meter is used on lemon cells joined in a row. One cell gives 0.9 volts, two give 1.8 volts and three give 2.7 volts. What is the rule? How many lemon cells match a pack of three AA cells, which gives 4.5 volts?
maths.answer: Each cell adds 0.9 volts. Five lemon cells give 4.5 volts.
maths.explain: The readings go up by 0.9 each time: 0.9, 1.8, 2.7. Carry on: four cells give 3.6 and five give 4.5. So five lemon cells push as hard as three AA cells.
maths.context: In the Lemon Battery test, lemon cells joined in a row made a louder crackle than one cell. These are made-up meter readings for such a row.
maths.why_maths: Finding the rule lets you say how many cells a job needs before you cut a single lemon.

maths.problem: Three lemon cells in a row should give 2.7 volts. A meter shows only 0.9 volts. Each cell gives 0.9 volts when tested alone. What is the likeliest reason?
maths.answer: One of the three cells is joined the wrong way round.
maths.explain: A cell that faces the other way pushes against the rest. So two cells add and one takes away: 0.9 plus 0.9 minus 0.9 is 0.9. If a cell were dead, the reading would be 1.8.
maths.context: In the Lemon Battery test, two lemon cells joined copper to copper gave no crackle, because their pushes cancelled. Here a row of three gives an odd reading on a meter.
maths.why_maths: Trying each possible fault with numbers shows which one fits the reading.

maths.problem: A lemon cell with zinc and copper gives 0.9 volts. A cell with kitchen foil and copper gives 0.5 volts. A red LED needs at least 1.8 volts. What is the smallest number of each kind of cell that will do?
maths.answer: Two zinc cells, or four foil cells.
maths.explain: Two zinc cells give 0.9 plus 0.9, which is 1.8 volts. Three foil cells give only 1.5 volts, which is too little. Four foil cells give 2.0 volts.
maths.context: In the Lemon Battery test you joined lemon cells in a row to light a red LED. Cells made with foil push less hard than cells made with zinc nails. These volts are typical values.
maths.why_maths: Adding decimals tells you how many cells of each kind you must build, and shows why foil needs more.

maths.problem: Bubbles are counted for 30 seconds while water is split. The minus pencil gives 24 bubbles and the plus pencil gives 12. How many times as many is that? At the same speed, how many would each give in 2 minutes?
maths.answer: Twice as many. In 2 minutes the minus pencil gives 96 bubbles and the plus pencil gives 48.
maths.explain: 24 divided by 12 is 2. Two minutes is four lots of 30 seconds. 24 times 4 is 96, and 12 times 4 is 48. The count is still two to one, because water has two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom.
maths.context: In Give It Back, four AA cells split water and bubbles rose from two pencil tips. The tip on the minus wire made more bubbles. These are made-up counts.
maths.why_maths: A ratio that stays the same however long you count points to something fixed, here the make-up of water.

maths.problem: The table shows rust scores for three nails in salt water over four days. Between which two days did the nail with copper rust fastest? On which day did the nail with zinc first show rust? What might have changed for the zinc that day?
maths.answer: The nail with copper rusted fastest between day 1 and day 2. The nail with zinc first showed rust on day 4, probably because its zinc was nearly used up.
maths.explain: The copper nail's score went from 0 to 2 in the first day. That is the biggest jump in the table. The zinc nail stayed at 0 for three days and reached 1 on day 4. Zinc protects only while there is zinc left to corrode.
maths.context: In the Bodyguard Nail, three steel nails sit in salt water for four days. One is alone, one touches zinc and one is wrapped in copper. Each day you give each nail a rust score. These scores are made up.
maths.why_maths: Looking at how fast each score changes shows when the protection started to fail. The last number alone does not show that.

maths.problem: A boat owner can bolt on new zinc blocks every year for 800 rupees. Without zinc, the steel rudder must be replaced every 3 years for 24,000 rupees. Which costs less over 6 years, and by how much?
maths.answer: The zinc costs 4,800 rupees and the rudders cost 48,000 rupees. The zinc is cheaper by 43,200 rupees.
maths.explain: Six years of zinc is 6 times 800, which is 4,800 rupees. In 6 years the rudder is replaced twice, and 2 times 24,000 is 48,000 rupees. 48,000 minus 4,800 is 43,200. The rudders cost ten times as much.
maths.context: In the Bodyguard Nail, a nail touching zinc stayed grey while a nail alone rusted. Boat owners protect steel hulls with zinc blocks in the same way. These prices are made up.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the cost over several years shows why people pay for a metal that only gets eaten.

quiz: Two copper wires in a lemon make a good battery.
The two metals must be different. Copper and copper give no push.
In a lemon cell, the zinc is slowly used up.
Zinc atoms give away electrons and leave the nail as ions.
Cells joined in a row push harder than one cell.
Their pushes add. Two cells of 1.5 volts give 3 volts.
An electric current can split water into two gases.
The gases are hydrogen and oxygen. This is called electrolysis.
Splitting water gives twice as much oxygen as hydrogen.
It gives twice as much hydrogen, because water has two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen atom.
Iron rusts in dry air with no water.
Rusting needs water as well as oxygen.
Salt water makes iron rust faster.
Salt water carries ions well, so the tiny cells on the iron work faster.
A coat of zinc protects steel even at a scratch.
Zinc gives electrons in place of the iron, as long as the two touch.
Gold is found in the ground as shiny metal.
Gold holds its electrons strongly, so it does not join with oxygen.

Charging is electrolysis. A current pushes the battery's change backwards.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1800 Alessandro Volta in Italy built the first battery. It was a pile of zinc and copper discs with wet card between them. Volta believed that the electricity came simply from two different metals touching. He thought the wet card only carried it, and that nothing was used up. News of the pile reached London within weeks. In May 1800, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle dipped its two wires into water. Bubbles rose from both wires. One gas was hydrogen and the other was oxygen. So electricity could cause a chemical change. Humphry Davy then argued the reverse: a chemical change inside the pile was making the electricity. He pointed out that the zinc discs were always eaten away. In the 1830s Michael Faraday settled the question by measuring. The amount of electricity a cell gave always matched the amount of zinc it lost. If touching alone made electricity, a battery would run for ever, and no battery does. Faraday had learned his first chemistry from a book by Jane Marcet.
how_we_found_out.who: Alessandro Volta, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle, Humphry Davy and Michael Faraday. Jane Marcet wrote Conversations on Chemistry, the book that first taught Faraday the subject.
how_we_found_out.when: Volta described his pile in 1800, and Nicholson and Carlisle split water in May 1800. Faraday published his measurements in 1834.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That two different metals make electricity just by touching, with nothing used up. Davy pointed out that the zinc is always eaten away. Faraday showed that the electricity a cell gives matches the zinc it loses.
how_we_found_out.art: A tall pile of grey and copper-coloured discs in a wooden frame on a table, with two wires from it dipping into a glass of water where bubbles rise from each wire.

roots.context: In this unit you made a lemon cell crackle, rusted a nail in ten minutes and split water. Here we ask what it means that a useful battery and a rusting gate are the same change.

deep_truth.truth: In the Lemon Battery test, the zinc nail gave away electrons and turned dull. In Rust in Ten Minutes, the nail that gave away electrons was eaten into rust. A rusting gate gives its electrons to oxygen in the same way. So a battery is a kind of corrosion in which the electrons are first sent through a wire.
deep_truth.habit: We put batteries with useful things that people make, and rust with damage and decay. They are one change. The only difference is whether the electrons pass through a wire, where they can do some work on the way.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Lemon Battery test, the earphones crackled only when a zinc nail and a copper wire shared the lemon. By the next day the zinc was dull and rough, and the copper was unchanged. In Rust in Ten Minutes, only the nail joined to the plus end of the cells turned to rust. That is the nail that the cells pulled electrons out of.

three.who_am_i: Your cells take electrons from your food and pass them to the oxygen you breathe. You stay alive because electrons keep moving through you.
three.what_is_life: Every living being, from a bacterium to a banyan tree, lives by passing electrons from one substance to another. A flame passes electrons from fuel to oxygen all at once. A living being does the same thing in many small steps.
three.what_is_this_world: A steel bridge is iron that people have pulled away from oxygen. The air and the rain slowly join the two again.

roots.thread: A battery, a rusting gate, a breathing child and a bacterium in mud look like four different things. In each of them, electrons leave one substance and go to another. The electron that lights an LED is the same kind of particle as the electron that rusts a nail. Many sages taught that one reality appears in many forms. The science here says something smaller and exact: several changes that we name separately are one kind of change.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son that by knowing one small tool of iron, all that is made of iron is known. The different forms are only names, and the truth is that all of them are iron.
teachings.link: The verse is about the one reality behind all things, and it uses iron as its picture. This unit found a small case of it. 'Battery', 'electrolysis' and 'rust' are three names. The passing of electrons is what all three are.

teachings.teaching: The chapter begins by saying that returning is how the Way moves.
teachings.link: The text is about nature as a whole, and it is not about chemistry. Yet every change in this unit could be turned back. Charging pushes a battery's change backwards. In Give It Back, the gases from split water joined again and made the earphones crackle. Rusting returns iron to what it was in the ground.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha says that all things that are put together are impermanent.
teachings.link: The verse is about how to live, and it is not about metals. Yet iron shows it plainly. Every iron thing is slowly going back to the oxide it was made from. Paint and zinc slow the return, and they do not end it.

science.text: Iron ore is iron joined to oxygen. Making steel separates the two, and rusting joins them again.

Living cells get their energy by passing electrons from food to oxygen in small steps. Peter Mitchell proposed in 1961 how cells use this passing. Jennifer Moyle's experiments helped prove it. It is found in almost all living things.
Life may have begun at deep-sea vents. Rocks and sea water there made a natural electrical difference, like the two sides of a cell.

other_view.view: To understand a thing, you must know what it is for, as well as what it is made of. A battery is made for a purpose, and rust is made for none. On this view, calling a battery and rust the same change leaves out what matters most about each.

practice.title: One breath, followed inwards
practice.say: Sit still and hold a steel spoon in your closed hand. Breathe in slowly. The oxygen you just took in is travelling to every cell of your body. In each cell it takes electrons that came from your food. Breathe out slowly. Now feel the spoon. It has grown warm from your hand. Some of that warmth comes from electrons passing to oxygen inside you. The spoon is steel, and it would take years of rain to pass its electrons to oxygen. Which of you two is changing faster?
practice.kid: Hold a steel spoon in your hand. Breathe in slowly, then out. Feel the spoon grow warm. Some of the warmth comes from electrons moving inside you.

playtest: Every experiment, activity and game was reasoned through step by step for a city flat. None has yet been tried at home. Please treat the expected results as predictions. The Lemon Battery test (core) needs 2 lemons, 4 galvanised nails and 4 pieces of bare copper wire. It also needs wired earphones with a round plug. A cell of zinc and copper gives about 0.9 volts, which makes a clear crackle. Two pieces of the same metal should give silence, or a very faint tick if one piece is dirtier. If you have only wireless earphones, use a red LED with four cells in a dark room, or a multimeter. Indian coins are steel, so they cannot stand in for copper. With foil in place of zinc nails the crackles are fainter and the LED may not glow. The zinc nail should be dull and dark the next day. Rust in Ten Minutes (core) uses four AA cells, which give 6 volts. That is safe to touch, but the bare wire ends must never touch each other. The plus nail should give a green-grey cloud within one or two minutes, turning brown. The nails must be plain steel. A galvanised nail gives a white cloud. Give It Back is the least certain. The crackle after the cells are removed should be clear but short, so test within five seconds. With only two cells it may be too faint. Electric Writing needs paper that is damp, not dripping. The Bodyguard Nail works best with a real galvanised nail. Foil protects less well. In the Kitchen Pile, foil and copper cells are weak, and the LED may not light. No part uses a wall socket, a charger or a 9-volt battery. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026: the 860 volts of the electric eel (2019 study), the Iron Pillar age and rust explanation, the Mars dust study of 2025, the paper and book citations (the page numbers of Davy 1824 were removed, and Marcet's year was corrected to 1805), and Volta's 1800 pile. The exact day of the first water splitting was softened to May 1800, and the museum gallery claim was softened. The volts given for lemon cells are typical values and will differ from lemon to lemon. The Baghdad jar is marked as a minority view. The Chandogya, Tao Te Ching and Dhammapada lines are paraphrases. The three videos have no address yet.
